60: Identity Verification
61: Monitor
62: Products available only on Custom plans
63: Layer
64: Signal Transaction Scores
65: Transfer
66: Plaid Check Consumer Report, except Base Report and Income Insights Report
67: Protect
68: Bank statement uploads for Document Income
69: Payment Initiation and Virtual Accounts (EU and UK only)
70: Consumer Report by Plaid Check
71: Consumer Report is available only to US entities evaluating US consumers.
72: Trial: Not available.
73: Pay-as-you-go: Not available.
74: Growth: Base Report and Income Insights Report, on request. Sole proprietorships need a Custom plan.
75: Custom: Everything in Consumer Report.
76: Trial plans
77: Free Trial plans are available to new Plaid teams (US/Canada only) created on or after April 15, 2026.
78: Using a Trial plan, you can use Plaid with real production data for free.
79: To start a Trial plan, create a Dashboard account and verify your email address. You can then access the Trial plan application form via the button on the Dashboard homepage or by going directly to https://dashboard.plaid.com/trial-plan.
80: Trial plan limitations
81: You can create 10 Production Items on a Trial plan. After creating 10 Items in Production, you must upgrade to a paid plan to create more Production Items. Removing Items created on a Trial plan (using /item/remove) will not allow you to create more Items.
82: You can see how many Production Items you have created on your Dashboard homepage.
83: When using a Trial plan, be sure to persist your access tokens and do not lose track of them. All access tokens created in Production will count against your Trial plan Item limit.
84: The following products are available via Trial plans:
85: Assets
86: Auth
87: Balance
88: Identity
89: Investments (including Investments Refresh)
90: Liabilities
91: Transactions (including Transactions Refresh)
92: Statements
93: If you added a subscription fee product (such as Investments, Liabilities, or Transactions) to an Item during your trial, upon upgrading to a paid plan, you will begin to be charged for that subscription.
94: Upon upgrading to a paid plan, you will only retain Production access to any products you explicitly requested in your Production request form. After upgrading, you may also need to request access to Fidelity in order to add additional Items at that institution. Requesting access and viewing your access status can both be done via the Dashboard OAuth institutions page.
95: Before creating your first Production Item, complete the Link setup steps in the launch checklist.
96: Pricing models
97: Plaid has multiple different pricing models, depending on the product. These models only apply to Production traffic; usage of Sandbox is always free.
98: Note that the details outlined below are general information and guidance about typical pricing structures and policies for new customers. Your specific pricing and billing structure is governed by your agreement with Plaid. If you have questions about your bill, contact support.
99: Endpoints that are not associated with any particular product are typically available to Plaid customers free of charge. Examples of these free-to-use endpoints include Institutions endpoints, Item endpoints, /accounts/get (not to be confused with /accounts/balance/get, which is associated with the Balance product), and user management endpoints.
100: One-time fee
101: Products that use one-time fee pricing are:
102: Auth
103: Identity
104: Income (except for /credit/payroll_income/refresh, which uses per-request pricing)
105: Layer
106: You will incur charges for one-time fee products whenever the product is successfully added to an Item. This occurs when an Item has been successfully created by Link and this product was specified in /link/token/create. An Item is typically considered to be successfully created if a public_token was exchanged, but sometimes (e.g. when using micro-deposit Auth flows, or the in-Link Identity Match flow) it may be considered created once the public_token was created. If the Item was not initialized with the product at the time of creation, the product can also be added to the Item later by calling a product endpoint belonging to that product on the Item.
107: For one-time fee products, it does not matter how many API calls are made for the Item (or user); the cost is the same regardless of whether the product's endpoints are called many times or zero times.
108: For the Auth and Identity products, if the product was added to the Item via the optional_products parameter in the /link/token/create call, you will not incur charges for those products until their corresponding endpoint is called. For example, if you initialize an Item with auth in the products parameter and identity in the optional_products parameter, you will not be charged for Identity on that Item until you call /identity/match or /identity/get for that access token. Note: Identity Match is a Per-request flat fee product, so calling /identity/match multiple times will result in repeated charges for Identity Match, but only one charge for Identity.
109: For a summary of how each product parameter in /link/token/create affects billing, see Initializing products during Link.
110: For Document Income and Payroll Income, charges will be incurred when data is available to be accessed. This will typically be indicated by the USER_INCOME_VERIFICATION webhook firing with the status of VERIFICATION_STATUS_PROCESSING_COMPLETE. Legacy integrations receive INCOME_VERIFICATION instead. For Document Income, the fee depends on the documents processed and which processing options are enabled (i.e. fraud, document parsing, or both). For bank statements, the fee is based on the number of pages in the statement; for all other document types, there is a flat fee per document.
111: For Hosted Link, each session delivered via SMS or email will incur a one-time fee. There is no fee to use Hosted Link if you are not using Plaid to deliver sessions.
112: When using Transfer, each Item initialized with Transfer (unless created using the /transfer/migrate_account endpoint) will also incur the one-time Auth fee, and no additional fee will be incurred for using Auth endpoints with that Item.
113: When using Layer, a billing event is incurred for each converted Link session (when onSuccess fires). You will not be billed for Layer eligibility checks or unconverted Layer sessions.
114: Subscription fee
115: Products that use subscription fee pricing are:
116: Transactions (except for the /transactions/refresh endpoint)
117: Recurring Transactions
118: Liabilities
119: Investments (except for the /investments/refresh endpoint)
120: Under the subscription fee model, an Item will incur a monthly subscription fee as long as a valid access_token exists for the Item. Removing the Item via /item/remove will end the subscription. Customers on user-based billing packages (this is not common) should call /user/products/terminate to end the subscription.
121: The subscription will also be ended if the end user depermissions their Item, such as via my.plaid.com or by contacting Plaid support. If the end user depermissions the Item via their financial institution's portal, this may also end the subscription, although this is not guaranteed, as not all institutions notify Plaid about permissions revocations performed via their portals.
122: Once a subscription fee product has been added to an Item, it is not possible to end the subscription and leave the Item in place. The Item must be deleted, which can be done by calling /item/remove. If the Item's subscription is active, Plaid will charge for the subscription even if no API calls are made for the Item or API calls cannot be successfully made for the Item (e.g. because the Item is in an error state). Plaid's subscription cycle is based on calendar months in the UTC time zone; each month begins a new cycle. Fees for Items created or removed in the middle of the month are not pro-rated. If you plan to delete unneedeed Items in bulk, ensure you begin the job early enough to fully complete before the next billing month begins, taking into account Plaid's rate limits.
123: If you add a subscription-billed product to an Item while on a Trial plan (for example, by creating an Item initialized with Transactions, Investments, or Liabilities), upon upgrading to a paid plan, you will begin to be charged for that subscription.
124: When using subscription fee products in Production, it is important to persist the access token so that you can remove the Item when needed to avoid being billed indefinitely. If you have created access tokens for which you are being billed but did not store the tokens, contact support for assistance.
125: A single Item can have multiple different subscriptions on it (for example, Transactions and Liabilities), but the same subscription will not be added multiple times to the same Item.
126: Investments has two separate subscriptions that can be associated with an Item: Investments Holdings and Investments Transactions. Adding Investments to an Item via /link/token/create or by calling /investments/holdings/get adds the Investments Holdings subscription. Calling /investments/transactions/get on an Item adds both the Investments Transactions and Investments Holdings subscriptions.
127: Per-request flat fee
128: For per-request flat fee products, a flat fee is charged for each successful API call to that product endpoint.
129: Products and endpoints that use per-request flat fee pricing are:
130: Balance (/accounts/balance/get; /signal/evaluate when used with a Balance-only ruleset)
131: Signal Transaction Scores (/signal/evaluate)
132: Investments Move (/investments/auth/get)
133: Transfer Signal or Balance fee (/transfer/authorization/create), see Transfer fee model for more details
134: Refresh endpoints, except for Statements Refresh (/transactions/refresh, /investments/refresh, /credit/payroll_income/refresh)
135: Asset report PDF and Audit Copy (/asset_report/audit_copy/create, /asset_report/pdf/get)
136: Identity Match (/identity/match), see below for more details
137: There is also a flat fee for each link delivered through SMS or email via Link Delivery (beta), when using Hosted Link with the optional Link Delivery feature enabled.
138: When calling /identity/match on an Item, in addition to the per-request Identity Match fee, the one-time Identity fee will be incurred if it has not already been incurred for that Item. Calling /identity/match multiple times on the same Item will result in repeated charges for Identity Match, but only one charge for Identity.
139: Identity Match can optionally be enabled via the Dashboard. In this integration mode, the Identity Match check is automatically performed during Link and you never call the /identity/match endpoint directly. The billing trigger for Identity Match in this situation is when Plaid successfully obtains Identity data from the Item. If Plaid could not obtain any Identity data for the Item, you will not be billed.
140: The /signal/evaluate endpoint is a billable endpoint that is used by two different products, Balance and Signal Transaction Scores. It will be billed as a Balance API call if used with a Balance-only ruleset. It will be billed as a Signal Transaction Scores API call if used with a Signal Transaction Scores–powered ruleset, or if used with no ruleset on a Signal Transaction Scores-enabled account.
141: Calls to /signal/evaluate that use a ruleset (including the default ruleset) will be billed when the ruleset is evaluated, even if some or all data could not be extracted from the Item.
142: Per-request flexible fee
143: Products that use per-request flexible fee pricing are:
144: Assets
145: Statements Refresh
146: Enrich
147: For per-request flexible fee products, a fee is charged for each successful API call to that product endpoint. The fee will vary depending on the amount of information requested in the API request.
148: For Assets, the fee is calculated based on the number of Items in the report as well as the number of days of history requested. An additional fee is charged for an Asset Report containing more than 5 Items; this fee will be charged twice if the Asset Report contains more than 10 Items, and so on. An "Additional History" fee is also charged for each Item for which more than 61 days of history is requested. The Additional History fee is a flat fee regardless of how many days of additional history are requested; it does not matter how many days beyond 61 are requested.
149: For Enrich, the flexible fee is based on the number of transactions sent to be enriched.
150: For /statements/refresh, the flexible fee is based on the number of statements available between the provided start and end dates found when calling /statements/refresh. Note that you will be charged for any statement extracted, even those that you previously requested at an earlier date.
151: Per-Item flexible fee
152: Products that use per-Item flexible fee pricing are:
153: Statements (excluding /statements/refresh, which is charged as a per-request flexible fee)
154: For per-Item flexible fee products, a fee is charged when the Item is created, which is deemed to occur when the public_token is created. The fee will vary depending on the amount of information requested when creating the Item.
155: For Statements, the flexible fee is calculated based on the number of statements available within the date range requested when calling /link/token/create. The fee will be charged even if you do not call any Statements endpoints.
156: Payment Initiation fee model
157: A fee is charged for each payment initiated. A payment is considered initiated if the end user reached the end of the payment flow and received a confirmation success screen. Standing orders (recurring payments) are considered a single payment but are billed on a separate pricing schedule from one-time payments. Fees will vary depending on the payment amount and the network used to transfer the payment.
158: Plaid Check fee model
159: Plaid Check (CRA) customers may be on bundle pricing or individual product pricing. If you are not sure which pricing model you are using, or to inquire about bundle pricing, contact your account manager.
160: Plaid Check bundle pricing
161: Plaid offers two Plaid Check (CRA) bundles:
162: Plaid Income — A suite of credit analytics to help lenders verify a user's income from their bank account. Includes Base Report and Income Insights.
163: Plaid Underwriting — A suite of credit analytics to help lenders assess risk and predict ability to pay. Includes Base Report, Cash Flow Insights, Network Insights, and LendScore.
164: With bundle pricing, the first time a billable Check Report endpoint (any endpoint ending in /get, such as /cra/check_report/base_report/get, /cra/check_report/income_insights/get, /cra/check_report/cashflow_insights/get, /cra/check_report/network_insights/get, /cra/check_report/lend_score/get, or /cra/check_report/pdf/get) is called for a given user_id or user_token, you will be charged the bundle fee. You can then call any Plaid Check endpoints within that bundle for the same user identifier within a 24-hour window at no additional charge.
165: After 24 hours, the user's report expires. Calls to product endpoints on an expired report will return a CONSUMER_REPORT_EXPIRED error. To continue calling product endpoints for that user, you must call /cra/check_report/create to generate a new Consumer Report. Once you create a new report and call a /get endpoint on it, you will be charged a new bundle fee, regardless of whether the original report has expired or not.
166: If you are subscribed to multiple bundles and only use products that overlap between those bundles (for example, calling only /cra/check_report/base_report/get when subscribed to both Plaid Income and Plaid Underwriting), you will be charged the lower of the applicable bundle fees.
167: Plaid Check individual product pricing
168: With individual product pricing, most Plaid Check (CRA) products are charged when the corresponding /get endpoint is called (/cra/check_report/base_report/get, /cra/check_report/income_insights/get, /cra/check_report/cashflow_insights/get, /cra/check_report/network_insights/get, /cra/check_report/lend_score/get, and /cra/check_report/pdf/get). The exception is Partner Insights, which is charged when the associated report is first generated and cra_partner_insights is specified in the product array, which can happen during /link/token/create or /cra/check_report/create.
169: There is no additional charge to call an endpoint multiple times if the same Consumer Report (the data snapshot generated when a user goes through Link or when /cra/check_report/create is called) is being retrieved each time. However, if a new Consumer Report is generated for a given user_id or user_token by calling /cra/check_report/create, a new set of fees will be incurred when a /get endpoint is called on the new report.
170: In addition to any product-specific charges, the first /get endpoint called for a given user_id or user_token and Consumer Report will also incur a Base Report charge. Note that /cra/check_report/network_insights/get is an exception: calling this endpoint does not trigger a Base Report charge.
171: For example, if you call /cra/check_report/base_report/get followed by /cra/check_report/income_insights/get, you will be charged the Base Report fee when the first endpoint is called and only the Income Insights fee when the second is called. If you call the endpoints in the reverse order, both the Base Report fee and the Income Insights fee will be charged when /cra/check_report/income_insights/get is called, and no fee will be charged when subsequently calling /cra/check_report/base_report/get.
172: After 24 hours, the user's report expires. Calls to product endpoints on an expired report will return a CONSUMER_REPORT_EXPIRED error. To continue calling product endpoints for that user, you must call /cra/check_report/create to generate a new Consumer Report. Once you create a new report and call a /get endpoint on it, you will be charged a new fee, regardless of whether the original report has expired or not.
173: When a new Consumer Report is created by calling /cra/check_report/create, a new set of fees will apply. The specific refresh fee incurred depends on which /get endpoint is called on the new report. For example, calling /cra/check_report/base_report/get after creating a new report incurs a Base Report Refresh fee; calling /cra/check_report/income_insights/get incurs an Income Insights Refresh fee.
174: Servicing pricing
175: Servicing is billed per subscribed user rather than per report. While a subscription is active, retrieving a report that the subscription generated does not incur a separate report charge.
176: Transfer fee model
177: When working with Transfer, there are three primary fees: The Auth fee, the Signal fee, and the per-transfer fee.
178: Existing contracts created or renewed prior to October 1, 2025 may contain references to a Transfer Risk Engine fee, which is assessed for each call to /transfer/authorization/create. For all new Transfer contracts going forward, this fee has been replaced with the Signal fee (which may also be called the Signal Transaction Scores fee or Balance fee, depending on which product(s) you are using).
179: Auth fee
180: When using Transfer, each Item with the Transfer product (unless created by the /transfer/migrate_account endpoint) will also have Auth added to the Item and will incur a one-time Auth fee in addition to the per-payment Transfer fee.
181: Signal fee
182: Calls to /transfer/authorization/create or /transfer/intent/create will incur per-request flat fees for Balance or Signal Transaction Scores, depending on the ruleset invoked. A fee is incurred for every successful invocation of a ruleset. However, if the authorization.decision returned in the response is user_action_required, you will not be charged.
183: Per-transfer fee
184: A fee is charged for each transfer made. A transfer is considered made if it was successfully created. This occurs when /transfer/create is successfully called, or if using Transfer UI instead of /transfer/create, when the onSuccess callback is fired from the Link session where the transfer is authorized. The per-transfer fee is charged even if the payment is later reversed or clawed back. In such cases, a reversed payment fee may be charged as well. Fees will vary depending on the payment amount and the network used to make the payment.
185: A per-transfer fee is also applied to funds transfers between your bank account and your balance held with Plaid, such as sweeps, or payments to and from the Plaid Ledger.
186: Operational fees
187: In addition to these product fees incurred by regular API activity, Transfer may charge operational fees for actions such as ACH returns, incoming wire transfers, and support requests for Plaid to perform certain actions such as providing a Written Statement of Unauthorized Debit (WSUD) or recalling or reversing a transfer. For more details, see ACH Transfer Investigations or contact your account manager.
188: Monitor fee model
189: Monitor uses a model with two fees:
190: A base fee, which is incurred the first time a new user is scanned
191: A rescanning fee, which is incurred based on the number of users rescanned each month
192: The rescanning fee is calculated based on the number of users on a rescanning program in a given month and works similarly to the subscription fee model. Plaid's subscription cycle is based on calendar months in the UTC time zone; each month begins a new cycle. Fees for users added to or removed from a rescanning program in the middle of the month are not pro-rated.
193: To avoid being rebilled for a user you no longer need recurring scans for (e.g., a user who has closed their account with you), create a program specifically for former users, make sure rescans are disabled, and move the user into that program when they are offboarded from your system.
194: Identity Verification fee model
195: For Identity Verification, a fee is charged based on the end user performing certain activities during the Link flow. The following events are billed:
196: Anti-Fraud Engine (the first verification check run, typically when the end user enters their phone number to begin SMS verification. If this is skipped, the Anti-Fraud Engine fee will be incurred later on. For example, if the SMS check is skipped in favor of the document check, the document check will incur both the Anti-Fraud Engine fee and the document check fee.)
197: Data Source verification (cost varies based on the end user's country, see your pricing contract for details)
198: Document check
199: Selfie check
200: If a retry is issued for a session, the retry will be billed like a new session, including the Anti-Fraud Engine and any other verification checks included in the retried session.
201: Partnerships pricing
202: If you are using a Plaid partner, you will be charged for Plaid API usage performed by the partner using your processor token in the same way as if the calls had been made by you. The partner's API usage will not be included in your Plaid Dashboard usage report. If you have questions about the partner's API activity, contact the Plaid partner.
203: Viewing billable activity and invoices
204: To view billable activity for your account, see the Production Usage page on the Dashboard.
205: Invoices will be sent each month to the billing contact configured for the team.
206: Updating payment information
207: Pay-as-you-go and Growth plan customers can update payment method and billing contact information on the Plaid Dashboard. Custom plan customers should contact their account manager to update this information.
208: Updating products
209: To view your currently enabled products, see the Products page in Dashboard Settings. To add additional products to your Plaid account you can submit the product request form located on the Dashboard. This form is also accessible via the Products page.
210: Viewing or changing pricing plans
211: To view current pricing or to switch between pricing plans, customers on Trial, Pay-as-you-go, or Growth plans can use the Plans page within the Dashboard. Customers with Trial or Pay-as-you-go plans can upgrade their plan at any time. Customers with Growth plans can submit a request to upgrade or downgrade their plan at any time; requests will take effect after the minimum commitment period on the existing Growth plan has been satisfied. Customers on Custom plans should contact support or their Plaid account manager.
212: Developer community
213: GitHub
214: YouTube
215: Discord

35: SDKs, and videos to help you build your Plaid integration.

38: you get started using Plaid!

58: A lending app using the Income API, using NodeJS and React
59: Demos, video tutorials, and guides
60: Demos
61: demo.plaid.com features interactive demos showing API calls alongside the end user experience for many Plaid products and use cases, including account funding and verification, personal financial management with Transactions, credit and underwriting, pay-by-bank, and more.
62: For the older demo page that just shows the Link UI rather than a full integration experience, see Link demo.
63: Video tutorials
64: Plaid Academy features detailed tutorial walkthroughs for common use cases and key concepts, several with accompanying repos.
65: Plaid in 3 Minutes contains overviews of different Plaid APIs, as well as short tutorials for busy people.
66: Plaid Quick Tips has snack-sized solutions to pressing Plaid problems.
67: The playlist below contains all of Plaid's up-to-date educational videos.
68: Launch center

70: make sure your app is Plaid-optimized and production ready.
71: Developer tools
72: Developer tools include our SDKs, Postman collection, and OpenAPI file.
73: SDKs

75: Plaid API and the Link frontend component, see libraries.
76: Postman
77: The Postman Collection provides an
78: easy, no-code way to explore the API.
79: Sandbox Studio
80: Sandbox Studio is a no-code way to explore Plaid
81: products from the Dashboard, using Sandbox test data.
82: OpenAPI file
83: The Plaid OpenAPI file is available on
84: GitHub. This file describes the Plaid API in a standardized way suitable for
85: usage with tools for testing, client library generation, and other purposes that
86: ingest OpenAPI/Swagger definition files.
87: Test data libraries
88: Sandbox Studio includes ready-made templates for
89: custom Sandbox users covering each product, which
90: you can use as-is or edit to test apps in Sandbox.
91: Enrich test transaction library
92: For testing Enrich, Plaid provides a list of Sandbox-compatible Enrich transactions.
93: Credit attributes library
94: For the Assets and Income products, Plaid maintains a
95: Credit attributes library of helper
96: scripts that can be used to derive various useful attributes from an Asset
97: Report or Bank Income.
98: AI developer tools
99: Plaid offers a number of tools to help you incorporate AI tooling into your development flow.
100: Plaid CLI
101: The Plaid CLI is a command-line interface for the Plaid API, designed for both developers and AI agents. Install via Homebrew, link a bank account, and start making API calls from the terminal. Pass --json for structured output that agents and scripts can parse directly.
102: Dashboard MCP server
103: Plaid's Dashboard MCP server allows you to access Plaid's diagnostics
104: and analytics tools to retrieve information about Link analytics, Item health, and more,
105: using your favorite LLM-powered application or client library.
106: Local MCP server
107: The Plaid AI coding toolkit ships with a local
108: MCP server that runs as a subprocess of your MCP client (Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code, Zed, etc.) and provides
109: helpful utilities for building and testing your Plaid-powered applications.
110: You can use it to generate realistic looking custom user data,
111: simulate webhooks, create public tokens in the Sandbox environment, or
112: search Plaid's documentation directly from your AI coding assistant so it can pull in the right context without
113: you pasting URLs. (Not to be confused with the Dashboard MCP server, a remote MCP server
114: hosted by Plaid that provides production diagnostics and analytics tools.)
115: LLM-friendly documentation
116: In accordance with the llms-txt proposal, an index of all
117: of Plaid's documentation can be found in LLM-friendly Markdown at
118: https://plaid.com/docs/llms.txt. You can find a Markdown equivalent of
119: Plaid documentation pages or API reference sections by clicking the document icon next to the header. You can also access Markdown pages by adding index.html.md to the end of the URL. For example, a Markdown version of https://plaid.com/docs/auth can be found at
120: https://plaid.com/docs/auth/index.html.md.
121: Consult the documentation for your favorite LLM-powered coding assistant
122: for the best way to incorporate this documentation into your workflow, as best
123: practices are changing frequently. Often, adding a prompt like the following
124: in your helper file can be useful.
125: Sample prompt
126: ## Instructions on using the Plaid API
127: For instructions on how to use the Plaid API, please go to
128: https://plaid.com/docs/llms.txt. There you can find a list of other
129: documentation pages that you can retrieve to obtain the necessary
130: information. If you need to search for additional documentation, you
131: should first try to use a link that is listed in the llms.txt file.
132: A single file containing all of Plaid's documentation can be found
133: at https://plaid.com/docs/llms-full.txt, although it is generally too large
134: to fit into most models' context windows.
135: Vibe coding guides
136: Trying to prompt your favorite LLM-powered coding tool to build a Plaid-powered
137: application? Plaid provides several detailed guides you
138: can reference within your LLM coding session that will provide your agent with
139: additional context. You can use these guides to more quickly build proof of concept
140: applications, or to kick-start your development process.
141: Vibe coding tips
142: Our vibe coding tips article contains recommendations on how to get your favorite AI coding assistant or IDE to work best with Plaid, including common mistakes AI tools will make and how to fix them.
143: Ask Bill
144: Bill is the helpful robot platypus that reads our docs for fun! You can ask Bill any time you need help with the Plaid API. Bill is also available as the search_documentation tool in the Plaid local MCP server, so he can search Plaid's docs from inside your AI coding assistant. Remember that Bill (like all of us) isn't perfect, even though he tries his best -- he can sometimes make mistakes, and he can only provide answers based on Plaid's published documentation and other publicly available information sources.
145: Community
146: You can join the
147: Plaid Developer Community on Discord.
148: Integration support
149: For small businesses and startups, HumbleDevs is a popular Plaid integration partner offering affordable integration solutions. HumbleDevs offers several pre-specced Plaid solutions packages with known timelines and costs for popular Plaid-powered solutions, and can also build a custom Plaid integration.
150: For larger businesses or those with other requirements, Plaid's partnerships team will work with you to understand your needs and recommend a partner that is a good fit for your business. For more information, contact your account manager or the sales team. Or, if you already have Production access, you can contact support and select "Building with Plaid" followed by "Plaid Partner Implementation Assistance".
151: At the enterprise level, Plaid also offers integration packages. For more details, contact sales or your account manager.

161: For a detailed chart showing Plaid's coverage by bank and product, see the US and Canada Bank Coverage Explorer and the European Bank Coverage Explorer.
162: Third-party resources
163: Several third party developers have built resources to help you integrate with
164: Plaid. Note that these resources are not built or supported by Plaid, and
165: inclusion of a resource on the list below does not constitute an endorsement by
166: Plaid or indicate that Plaid has evaluated the resource for correctness,
167: security, or anything else.
168: If you have a third-party resource you'd like to be featured on this list, DM us
169: @plaiddev on X, or reach out to an admin
170: on the Plaid Developer Discord.
171: How to Build a Fintech app on AWS using the Plaid API
172: and the accompanying
173: sample app demonstrates
174: how to build a Plaid app on AWS, using the latest Transactions Sync API. The
175: app and tutorial incorporate AWS Lambda for webhook handling and Amazon
176: Cognito for authentication.
177: The Plaid tag on GitHub contains multiple example apps using Plaid.
178: WebhookDB has a tutorial showing how to
179: use their service to manage Plaid webhooks.
180: The CloudQuery Plaid plugin
181: extracts data from Plaid and loads it into any supported CloudQuery
182: destination, such as PostgreSQL, Snowflake, BigQuery, or S3.
183: Developer community
184: GitHub
185: YouTube
186: Discord

34: Ask a question...
35: Hi! I'm Bill! You can ask me all about the Plaid API. Try asking questions like:Pssst -- I also moonlight as your IDE's research librarian! Plug me in via the Plaid MCP Server.
36: Note: Bill isn't perfect. He's just a robot platypus that reads our docs for fun. You should treat his answers with the same healthy skepticism you might treat any other answer on the internet. This chat may be logged for quality and training purposes. Please don't send Bill any PII -- he's scared of intimacy. All chats with Bill are subject to Plaid's Privacy Policy.
37: Launch in Production checklist
38: Check off these recommended steps before launching your app in Production
39: The Launch Checklist has been replaced by the Launch Center. The Launch Center shows a personalized list of steps for your integration, with links to supporting materials like videos, sample code, and docs. The Launch Checklist is no longer being updated.
40: Below is a list of recommended steps to take before launching your Plaid integration in production. While they might not all be required for the minimal operation of your application, the steps below will help to make your Plaid integration more robust, secure, efficient, and maintainable.
41: Production setup
42: If you haven't already done so, request Production access.
43: Complete your application profile and company profile, which are required to access certain institutions that use OAuth-based connections.
44: Complete your security questionnaire, which is required to access certain US institutions that use OAuth-based connections.
45: For European Union countries and the UK, there is a separate compliance process required to access financial institutions in Production. If your Plaid integration will support financial institutions in Europe (including the UK), and your business is not based in Europe, file a support ticket to request Production access for Europe. Allow at least one week for your request to be processed.
46: Configure both Plaid Link and your server-side code to use the Production
47: environment by setting the appropriate value when configuring your client object or (if not using a client library) your HTTP request. For language-specific details, see the GitHub page for your client library, or API host information if not using a library.
48: Ensure you are using your Production secret, which can be found on the dashboard.
49: If migrating from Sandbox, ensure that you remove any usage of Sandbox-specific functionality, such as the user_good test user or calls to /sandbox/ endpoints.
50: Add teammates to the dashboard to give other users access. For more details, see Plaid teams.
51: Link setup
52: Follow the steps below to assist users in completing the Link flow, help ensure compliance with Plaid's policies, and avoid being billed for unneeded products.
53: Implement OAuth support. Some institutions in both Europe and the US require the use of OAuth-based connections. While OAuth will typically "just work" on desktop, as long as you have completed your application profile, company profile, and security questionnaire, you may need to implement client-side redirect logic for users on mobile devices.
54: Make sure your OAuth integration works with all the test cases recommended in the OAuth documentation.
55: Add every redirect_uri you pass to /link/token/create to the Allowed redirect URIs in the Dashboard. Production redirect URIs must use HTTPS. See Create and register a redirect URI.
56: To avoid unnecessary billing and user confusion, implement logic for preventing duplicate Items.
57: Configure Link customizations within the
58: dashboard and ensure that the countries and languages selected for the customizations match the settings provided to /link/token/create. For more details, see Link customization.
59: For Link sessions in the US or Canada, select a use case under Data Transparency Messaging in the Link customization UI. Trial plans use a default use case, so this applies once you're on a paid plan.
60: Ensure the client_name parameter of /link/token/create is set
61: to display your company's name as you'd like it to appear within Link.
62: Ensure that the products parameter of /link/token/create includes only the
63: products you intend to use. The products listed here will influence which
64: institutions and accounts appear in Link (only institutions and account types that support all specified products will
65: appear in Link) and will trigger a billing event for listed products upon
66: successful token exchange.
67: If you are using multiple Plaid products, see the recommendations in Choosing how to initialize products to make sure your Link sessions are optimized for performance, conversion, and billing.
68: If you plan to use a product later but aren't initializing it in Link, list it in the additional_consented_products parameter of /link/token/create. Otherwise, calling its endpoints on the Item can fail with ADDITIONAL_CONSENT_REQUIRED. See Adding products post-Link.
69: Provide any notice and obtain any consent required for Plaid to process end user
70: information in accordance with Plaid's End User Privacy Policy.
71: You may find it helpful to know that some of our customers link to Plaid's privacy policy within their own privacy policy, while others surface a separate just-in-time notice and consent page during their onboarding flow. Ultimately, it is up to you to determine how to obtain any legally required consents.
72: To maximize the number of users who complete the Link flow, review Plaid's recommendations for optimizing Link conversion and implement any practices relevant to your use case, such as providing pre-Link messaging.
73: Callbacks
74: Handle callbacks beyond just onSuccess in order to gracefully handle errors and build analytics around Link.
75: Listen to the onExit() and onEvent() callbacks for error_type and error_code in order to implement error handling.
76: Listen to the onEvent() callback for
77: exit_status or timestamp in order to implement Link conversion analytics. Alternatively, you can use Plaid's built-in Link conversion analytics in the Dashboard.
78: Webhook configuration
79: Plaid uses webhooks for many common flows. If your integration does any of the following, webhooks are required or strongly recommended:
80: (Any product) Your application is calling a Plaid endpoint for an Item repeatedly, over a period of time, not just immediately after Link.
81: (Transactions or Investments) You are accessing transactions made after the end user linked their Item.
82: (Auth) You are using automated micro-deposits for account verification, or making transfers over a year after the Item was initially linked.
83: (Assets) You are creating Asset Reports.
84: (Income) You are verifying a user's income.
85: (Payment Initiation (UK and Europe)) You are initiating payments.
86: (Virtual Accounts (UK and Europe) or Transfer) You are sending or receiving funds.
87: Make sure Link has been initialized with your URL for receiving webhooks via /link/token/create.
88: (For Identity Verification, Transfer or Payment Initiation, as well as optional Auth micro-deposit events) Make sure to configure account level webhook URLs via the Plaid Dashboard.
89: Make sure you can receive webhooks from Plaid's webhook IPs.
90: Review Plaid's webhook best practices to ensure your webhook handling logic is robust to outages and traffic spikes.
91: For all Item-based products, listen for the PENDING_DISCONNECT webhook and send the Item through update mode when receiving it.
92: Error handling
93: Sometimes, Plaid API calls may fail due to intermittent outages or connectivity errors at supported institutions. Implement retry logic or error handling as necessary for product API calls.
94: Link in update mode
95: Update mode is used to fix Items that have entered an error state (for example, because a user changed their password). If your application needs to access an Item repeatedly over a period of time, rather than just immediately after Link, implementing update mode logic is strongly recommended.
96: Handle the ITEM_LOGIN_REQUIRED, PENDING_DISCONNECT, and PENDING_EXPIRATION Item errors or webhooks by launching update mode to ensure your users retain access to their Items. For more information, see Updating Items via Link.
97: Listen for the NEW_ACCOUNTS_AVAILABLE webhook to learn when an Item has a new account associated with it. To request access to that account, launch Link in update mode.
98: (Optional, Auth and Identity only) Implement Product Validations in update mode to prevent customers from accidentally revoking required permissions during the update mode flow.
99: Storage & logging
100: Log Plaid identifiers and IDs properly to enhance security, when contacting Support about a specific request or callback, and for finding specific entries in the Activity Log. For more information, see Dashboard logs and troubleshooting.
101: Access tokens and Item IDs are the core identifiers that map your users to
102: their financial institutions. Store them securely and associate them with
103: users of your application. Make sure, however, that these identifiers are
104: never exposed client-side. Keep in mind that one user can create multiple
105: Items if they have accounts with multiple financial institutions.
106: The same storage requirements apply to other identifiers used instead of access tokens by certain products, such as asset report tokens (used with Assets), payment profile tokens (used with Transfer), and user IDs (or user tokens for legacy integrations) used with Income.
107: Ensure that the following identifiers are securely logged, as they will be needed when contacting Support about a specific request or callback.
108: link_session_id: Included in the onExit, onEvent, and onSuccess callback of a Link integration.
109: request_id: Included in all Plaid API responses.
110: account_id: Included in all successful Plaid API responses that relate to a specific Item or account.
111: item_id: Included in all successful Plaid API responses that relate to a specific Item.
112: Item management
113: Delete Items using /item/remove when they are no longer being used. For example, you may wish to allow users to remove linked Items through your app's account management interface, or you may want to delete Items when a user deletes their account with your service or becomes inactive, or if the Item has been in an error state for an extended period. Deleting unneeded Items is a security best practice and will also prevent you from being charged for these Items when using a subscription-based product such as Transactions.
114: Multi-app use cases
115: If you anticipate having multiple apps that use Plaid or having multiple teams at your company using it, consider creating a single shared backend service to handle functions such as logging and token storage in a consolidated place.
116: Product-specific recommendations
117: Auth
118: If launching in the US, support the Automated Micro-deposits and Same-Day Micro-deposits flows for maximum institution coverage.
119: If supporting the Instant Match, Automated Micro-deposits, or Same-Day Micro-deposits flows, make sure that the country codes parameter provided to /link/token/create for these flows includes only the US and no other countries.
120: If supporting the Automated Micro-deposits flow, make sure to listen for Auth webhooks to know when the transaction is completed.
121: Make sure you are not displaying account numbers in your app's UI, even if truncated or masked, to avoid user confusion when working with institutions that provide virtualized or temporary account numbers. Always use values from the mask field instead.
122: Listen for the USER_ACCOUNT_REVOKED and USER_PERMISSION_REVOKED webhooks to be notified when a temporary account number has become invalidated. To avoid R04 errors, do not make a transfer using an account number, processor token, or Stripe bank account token that has been revoked. Instead, send the user through update mode to restore the Item; if update mode cannot be launched (which can occur for USER_PERMISSION_REVOKED), create a new Item instead. Then call the auth endpoint again to obtain a new account number or token.
123: Listen for the AUTH: DEFAULT_UPDATE webhook to be notified when an Item's account or routing number has changed, then call /auth/get or /processor/auth/get again to refresh your information on file.
124: Balance
125: If you are using Balance with non-depository accounts, such as credit card or loan accounts, make sure to specify min_last_updated_datetime when calling /accounts/balance/get to ensure balance calls to Capital One can succeed.
126: Identity
127: Transactions
128: If fetching historical Transactions data using /transactions/get or /transactions/sync, make sure your app implements pagination logic. For sample code, see the integration instructions or the API Reference for the endpoint.
129: If you use /transactions/sync, make sure your app properly handles errors that occur during pagination by restarting the pagination loop. For more details, see TRANSACTIONS_SYNC_MUTATION_DURING_PAGINATION.
130: Handle Transactions webhooks, see Handling Transaction webhooks.
131: Investments
132: Handle the HOLDINGS-type DEFAULT_UPDATE webhook if your app needs to keep holdings, values, and balances up-to-date.
133: Handle the INVESTMENTS_TRANSACTIONS-type DEFAULT_UPDATE webhook if your app needs to keep Investments transactions up-to-date.
134: Handle the INVESTMENTS_TRANSACTIONS-type HISTORICAL_UPDATE webhook to know when an Item's full investment transaction history is available, and call /investments/transactions/get again when it fires. For details, see Investments transactions initialization behavior.
135: If fetching historical Investments transactions using /investments/transactions/get, make sure your app implements pagination logic. For sample code, see the /investments/transactions/get API Reference (pagination examples available in Python and Ruby code samples).
136: Assets
137: Handle the ASSETS-type PRODUCT_READY webhook to know when to call /asset_report/get.
138: Handle the ASSETS-type ERROR webhook to gracefully handle errors from failures in /asset_report/create.
139: Payment Initiation
140: Handle the PAYMENT_STATUS_UPDATE webhook to keep updated on payment status information.
141: Virtual Accounts
142: Handle the WALLET_TRANSACTION_STATUS_UPDATE webhook to keep updated on transaction status information.
143: Income
144: Handle the INCOME-type USER_INCOME_VERIFICATION webhook to know when the verification is complete and endpoints that show income or employment related data are ready to be called. Existing integrations that have not migrated should continue handling the legacy INCOME_VERIFICATION webhook.
145: Identity Verification
146: Make sure to update your template IDs when moving to Production; the Sandbox and Production environments have different template IDs.
147: If you've set any of your Acceptable Risk Levels to "high" in your Risk Rules in order to prevent checks from failing during testing, make sure to change them back to the levels you plan to use in Production.
148: Implement logic for users to retry identity verification if they have failed.
149: You can integrate this process directly using the /identity_verification/retry
150: endpoint or from the Dashboard.
151: If enabling Selfie Check, make sure that you are requesting the required camera permissions on mobile.
152: When performing your matching logic, make sure to take into account that no_data is
153: different from no_match. no_data means that the list issuer didn't supply data
154: against which to match. no_match means that data was provided by the list issuer
155: and it did not match the information provided by your customer.
156: Monitor
157: Make sure to implement logic for both onboarding (adding users to a program when they are created) and offboarding (moving users to a program with rescans disabled when they close their account).
158: Ensure that the Monitor review queue is checked regularly. For more details, see Building a reviewer workflow and preparing for ongoing screening.
159: Developer community
160: GitHub
161: YouTube
162: Discord

1: # mcp-server-plaid: A Plaid MCP server
2: ## Overview
3: A Model Context Protocol server for facilitating integration with Plaid. This server provides tools to generate mock financial data, search Plaid documentation, and interact with sandbox APIs for testing purposes.
4: ### Tools
5: 1. `search_documentation`
6: - Search Plaid documentation for relevant information about products or API endpoints using with the help of Bill, the friendly robot platypus who reads our docs for fun.
7: - Returns: Detailed information from Plaid's documentation
8: 2. `get_mock_data_prompt`
9: - Return prompt to generate customized mock financial data for testing
10: 3. `get_sandbox_access_token`
11: - Obtain a working access token for the Plaid sandbox environment
12: - Returns: Access token and item ID for testing with sandbox mocked data
13: 4. `simulate_webhook`
14: - Simulate a Plaid webhook event in the sandbox environment
15: - Useful for testing your application's webhook handling
16: - Returns: Webhook fired status and status code
17: ## Configuration
18: ### Obtaining API Credentials
19: 1. Sign in to your [Plaid Developer Dashboard](https://dashboard.plaid.com) account
20: 2. Navigate to **Developers** → **[Keys](https://dashboard.plaid.com/developers/keys)**
21: 3. Locate your **sandbox credentials**.
22: > [!IMPORTANT]
23: > All `PLAID_CLIENT_ID` and `PLAID_SECRET` references in the following MCP configuration use **sandbox credentials**.
24: > [!NOTE]
25: > All snippets below use `uvx`. If you installed via pip, swap `uvx mcp-server-plaid` for `python -m mcp_server_plaid`.
26: ### Usage with Claude Code
27: Add this to `.mcp.json` in your project root (or `~/.claude.json` for a user-scoped install):
28: ```json
29: {
30: "mcpServers": {
31: "plaid": {
32: "command": "uvx",
33: "args": [
34: "mcp-server-plaid",
35: "--client-id",
36: "YOUR_PLAID_CLIENT_ID",
37: "--secret",
38: "YOUR_PLAID_SECRET"
39: ]
40: }
41: }
42: }
43: ```
44: Or use the CLI:
45: ```bash
46: claude mcp add plaid -- uvx mcp-server-plaid --client-id YOUR_PLAID_CLIENT_ID --secret YOUR_PLAID_SECRET
47: ```
48: ### Usage with Cursor
49: For quick installation, use the one-click installation button.
50: [![Install MCP Server](https://cursor.com/deeplink/mcp-install-dark.svg)](https://cursor.com/en/install-mcp?name=plaid&config=eyJjb21tYW5kIjoidXZ4IiwiYXJncyI6WyJtY3Atc2VydmVyLXBsYWlkIl0sImVudiI6eyJQTEFJRF9DTElFTlRfSUQiOiJBRERfWU9VUl9DTElFTlRfSUQiLCJQTEFJRF9TRUNSRVQiOiJBRERfWU9VUl9BUElfU0VDUkVUIn19)
51: For manual installation, add the following JSON block to Cursor MCP config file.
52: ```json
53: {
54: "mcpServers": {
55: "plaid": {
56: "command": "uvx",
57: "args": [
58: "mcp-server-plaid",
59: "--client-id",
60: "YOUR_PLAID_CLIENT_ID",
61: "--secret",
62: "YOUR_PLAID_SECRET"
63: ]
64: }
65: }
66: }
67: ```
68: ### Usage with Codex
69: Add this to `~/.codex/config.toml`:
70: ```toml
71: [mcp_servers.plaid]
72: command = "uvx"
73: args = ["mcp-server-plaid", "--client-id", "YOUR_PLAID_CLIENT_ID", "--secret", "YOUR_PLAID_SECRET"]
74: ```
75: ### Usage with VS Code
76: For quick installation, use one of the one-click installation buttons below.
77: [![Install with UV in VS Code](https://img.shields.io/badge/VS_Code-UV-0098FF?style=flat-square&logo=visualstudiocode&logoColor=white)](https://insiders.vscode.dev/redirect/mcp/install?name=plaid&inputs=%5B%7B%22type%22%3A%22promptString%22%2C%22id%22%3A%22client_id%22%2C%22description%22%3A%22Plaid%20Client%20ID%22%2C%22password%22%3Afalse%7D%2C%7B%22type%22%3A%22promptString%22%2C%22id%22%3A%22secret%22%2C%22description%22%3A%22Plaid%20Secret%22%2C%22password%22%3Atrue%7D%5D&config=%7B%22command%22%3A%22uvx%22%2C%22args%22%3A%5B%22mcp-server-plaid%22%5D%2C%22env%22%3A%7B%22PLAID_CLIENT_ID%22%3A%22%24%7Binput%3Aclient_id%7D%22%2C%22PLAID_SECRET%22%3A%22%24%7Binput%3Asecret%7D%22%7D%7D) [![Install with UV in VS Code Insiders](https://img.shields.io/badge/VS_Code_Insiders-UV-24bfa5?style=flat-square&logo=visualstudiocode&logoColor=white)](https://insiders.vscode.dev/redirect/mcp/install?name=plaid&inputs=%5B%7B%22type%22%3A%22promptString%22%2C%22id%22%3A%22client_id%22%2C%22description%22%3A%22Plaid%20Client%20ID%22%2C%22password%22%3Afalse%7D%2C%7B%22type%22%3A%22promptString%22%2C%22id%22%3A%22secret%22%2C%22description%22%3A%22Plaid%20Secret%22%2C%22password%22%3Atrue%7D%5D&config=%7B%22command%22%3A%22uvx%22%2C%22args%22%3A%5B%22mcp-server-plaid%22%5D%2C%22env%22%3A%7B%22PLAID_CLIENT_ID%22%3A%22%24%7Binput%3Aclient_id%7D%22%2C%22PLAID_SECRET%22%3A%22%24%7Binput%3Asecret%7D%22%7D%7D&quality=insiders)
78: For manual installation, add the following JSON block to your user `mcp.json` file in VS Code. You can do this by pressing `Ctrl + Shift + P` and typing `MCP: Open User Configuration`.
79: Optionally, you can add it to a file called `.vscode/mcp.json` in your workspace. This will allow you to share the configuration with others.
80: ```json
81: {
82: "inputs": [
83: {
84: "type": "promptString",
85: "id": "client_id",
86: "description": "Plaid Client ID",
87: "password": false
88: },
89: {
90: "type": "promptString",
91: "id": "secret",
92: "description": "Plaid Secret",
93: "password": true
94: }
95: ],
96: "servers": {
97: "plaid": {
98: "command": "uvx",
99: "args": ["mcp-server-plaid"],
100: "env": {
101: "PLAID_CLIENT_ID": "${input:client_id}",
102: "PLAID_SECRET": "${input:secret}"
103: }
104: }
105: }
106: }
107: ```
108: ### Usage with Claude Desktop
109: Add this to your `claude_desktop_config.json`:
110: ```json
111: {
112: "mcpServers": {
113: "plaid": {
114: "command": "uvx",
115: "args": [
116: "mcp-server-plaid",
117: "--client-id",
118: "YOUR_PLAID_CLIENT_ID",
119: "--secret",
120: "YOUR_PLAID_SECRET"
121: ]
122: }
123: }
124: }
125: ```
126: ### Usage with Zed
127: Add to your Zed `settings.json`:
128: ```json
129: {
130: "context_servers": {
131: "mcp-server-plaid": {
132: "command": {
133: "path": "uvx",
134: "args": [
135: "mcp-server-plaid",
136: "--client-id",
137: "YOUR_PLAID_CLIENT_ID",
138: "--secret",
139: "YOUR_PLAID_SECRET"
140: ]
141: }
142: }
143: }
144: }
145: ```
146: ## Debugging
147: You can use the MCP inspector to debug the server. For uvx installations:
148: ```
149: npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector uvx mcp-server-plaid --client-id YOUR_PLAID_CLIENT_ID --secret YOUR_PLAID_SECRET
150: ```
151: Or if you've installed the package in a specific directory or are developing on it:
152: ```
153: cd sandbox
154: npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector uv run mcp-server-plaid --client-id YOUR_PLAID_CLIENT_ID --secret YOUR_PLAID_SECRET
155: ```
156: ## License
157: This MCP server is licensed under the MIT License. This means you are free to use, modify, and distribute the software, subject to the terms and conditions of the MIT License. For more details, please see the LICENSE file in the project repository.

[Query relevant filters (USER_DATA)](#query-relevant-filters-user_data) 75: 76: 77: 78: # Public Rest API for Binance 79: ## General API Information 80: - The following base endpoints are available. Please use whichever works best for your setup: 81: - **https://api.binance.com** 82: - **https://api-gcp.binance.com** 83: - **https://api1.binance.com** 84: - **https://api2.binance.com** 85: - **https://api3.binance.com** 86: - **https://api4.binance.com** 87: - The last 4 endpoints in the point above (`api1`-`api4`) should give better performance but have 88: less stability. 89: - Responses are in JSON by default. To receive responses in SBE, refer to the 90: [SBE FAQ](faqs/sbe_faq.md) page. 91: - Data is returned in **chronological order**, unless noted otherwise. 92: - Without `startTime` or `endTime`, returns the most recent items up to the limit. 93: - With `startTime`, returns oldest items from `startTime` up to the limit. 94: - With `endTime`, returns most recent items up to `endTime` and the limit. 95: - With both, behaves like `startTime` but does not exceed `endTime`. 96: - All time and timestamp related fields in the JSON responses are in **milliseconds by default.** To 97: receive the information in microseconds, please add the header `X-MBX-TIME-UNIT:MICROSECOND` or 98: `X-MBX-TIME-UNIT:microsecond`. 99: - We support HMAC, RSA, and Ed25519 keys. For more information, please see 100: [API Key types](faqs/api_key_types.md). 101: - Timestamp parameters (e.g. `startTime`, `endTime`, `timestamp`) can be passed in milliseconds or 102: microseconds. 103: - For APIs that only send public market data, please use the base endpoint 104: **https://data-api.binance.vision**. Please refer to 105: [Market Data Only](faqs/market_data_only.md) page. 106: - If there are enums or terms you want clarification on, please see the 107: [SPOT Glossary](faqs/spot_glossary.md) for more information. 108: - APIs have a timeout of 10 seconds when processing a request. If a response from the Matching 109: Engine takes longer than this, the API responds with "Timeout waiting for response from backend 110: server. Send status unknown; execution status unknown." 111: [(-1007 TIMEOUT)](errors.md#-1007-timeout) 112: - This does not always mean that the request failed in the Matching Engine. 113: - If the status of the request has not appeared in 114: [User Data Stream](user-data-stream.md), please perform an API query for its status. 115: - **Please avoid SQL keywords in requests** as they may trigger a security block by a WAF (Web 116: Application Firewall) rule. See https://www.binance.com/en/support/faq/detail/360004492232 for 117: more details. 118: - If your request contains a symbol name containing non-ASCII characters, then the response may 119: contain non-ASCII characters encoded in UTF-8. 120: - Some endpoints may return asset and/or symbol names containing non-ASCII characters encoded in 121: UTF-8 even if the request did not contain non-ASCII characters. 122: ## HTTP Return Codes 123: - HTTP `4XX` return codes are used for malformed requests; the issue is on the sender's side. 124: - HTTP `403` return code is used when a WAF (Web Application Firewall) rule has been violated. This 125: can indicate a rate limit violation or a security block. See 126: https://www.binance.com/en/support/faq/detail/360004492232 for more details. 127: - HTTP `409` return code is used when a cancelReplace order partially succeeds. (i.e. if the 128: cancellation of the order fails but the new order placement succeeds.) 129: - HTTP `429` return code is used when breaking a request rate limit. 130: - HTTP `418` return code is used when an IP has been auto-banned for continuing to send requests 131: after receiving `429` codes. 132: - HTTP `5XX` return codes are used for internal errors; the issue is on Binance's side. It is 133: important to **NOT** treat this as a failure operation; the execution status is **UNKNOWN** and 134: could have been a success. 135: ## Error Codes 136: - Any endpoint can return an ERROR 137: Sample Payload below: 138: ```javascript 139: { 140: "code": -1121, 141: "msg": "Invalid symbol." 142: } 143: ``` 144: - Specific error codes and messages are defined in [Errors Codes](errors.md). 145: ## General Information on Endpoints 146: - For `GET` endpoints, parameters must be sent as a `query string`. 147: - For `POST`, `PUT`, and `DELETE` endpoints, the parameters may be sent as a `query string` or in 148: the `request body` with content type `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`. You may mix parameters 149: between both the `query string` and `request body` if you wish to do so. 150: - Parameters may be sent in any order. 151: - If a parameter sent in both the `query string` and `request body`, the `query string` parameter 152: will be used. 153: 154: ## Conditional fields in Order Responses 155: There are fields in the order responses (e.g. order placement, order query, order cancellation) that 156: appear only if certain conditions are met. 157: These fields can apply to order lists. 158: The fields are listed below: 159: | Field | Description | Visibility conditions | Examples | 160: | ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | 161: | `icebergQty` | Quantity for the iceberg order | Appears only if the parameter `icebergQty` was sent in the request. | `"icebergQty": "0.00000000"` | 162: | `quoteNotionalLimit` | Maximum quote-asset notional the order may consume | Appears only if the order was placed with a quote notional limit. | `"quoteNotionalLimit": "250.00000000"` | 163: | `preventedMatchId` | When used in combination with `symbol`, can be used to query a prevented match. | Appears only if the order expired due to STP. | `"preventedMatchId": 0` | 164: | `preventedQuantity` | Order quantity that expired due to STP | Appears only if the order expired due to STP. | `"preventedQuantity": "1.200000"` | 165: | `effectiveSelfTradePreventionMode` | Self-trade-prevention mode the engine actually applied. Cause of the order’s expiration | When an order has expired | `"expiryReason": "INSUFFICIENT_LIQUIDITY"` | 178: ## LIMITS 179: ### General Info on Limits 180: - The following `intervalLetter` values for headers: 181: - SECOND => S 182: - MINUTE => M 183: - HOUR => H 184: - DAY => D 185: - `intervalNum` describes the amount of the interval. For example, `intervalNum` 5 with 186: `intervalLetter` M means "Every 5 minutes". 187: - The `/api/v3/exchangeInfo` `rateLimits` array contains objects related to the exchange's 188: `RAW_REQUESTS`, `REQUEST_WEIGHT`, and `ORDERS` rate limits. These are further defined in the 189: `ENUM definitions` section under `Rate limiters (rateLimitType)`. 190: - Requests fail with HTTP status code 429 when you exceed the request rate limit. 191: ### IP Limits 192: - Every request will contain `X-MBX-USED-WEIGHT-(intervalNum)(intervalLetter)` in the response 193: headers which has the current used weight for the IP for all request rate limiters defined. 194: - Each route has a `weight` which determines for the number of requests each endpoint counts for. 195: Heavier endpoints and endpoints that do operations on multiple symbols will have a heavier 196: `weight`. 197: - When a 429 is received, it's your obligation as an API to back off and not spam the API. 198: - **Repeatedly violating rate limits and/or failing to back off after receiving 429s will result in 199: an automated IP ban (HTTP status 418).** 200: - IP bans are tracked and **scale in duration** for repeat offenders, **from 2 minutes to 3 days**. 201: - A `Retry-After` header is sent with a 418 or 429 responses and will give the **number of seconds** 202: required to wait, in the case of a 429, to prevent a ban, or, in the case of a 418, until the ban 203: is over. 204: - **The limits on the API are based on the IPs, not the API keys.** 205: ### Unfilled Order Count 206: - Every successful order response will contain a `X-MBX-ORDER-COUNT-(intervalNum)(intervalLetter)` 207: header indicating how many orders you have placed for that interval.

To monitor this, 208: refer to 209: [`GET api/v3/rateLimit/order`](rest-api.md#query-unfilled-order-count-user_data). 210: - Rejected/unsuccessful orders are not guaranteed to have `X-MBX-ORDER-COUNT-**` headers in the 211: response. 212: - If you have exceeded this, you will receive a 429 error with the `Retry-After` header. 213: - **Please note that if your orders are consistently filled by trades, you can continuously place 214: orders on the API**. For more information, please see 215: [Spot Unfilled Order Count Rules](faqs/order_count_decrement.md). 216: - **The number of unfilled orders is tracked for each account.** 217: ## Data Sources 218: - The API system is asynchronous, so some delay in the response is normal and expected. 219: - Each endpoint has a data source indicating where the data is being retrieved, and thus which 220: endpoints have the most up-to-date response. 221: These are the three sources, ordered by least to most potential for delays in data updates. 222: - **Matching Engine** - the data is from the Matching Engine 223: - **Memory** - the data is from a server's local or external memory 224: - **Database** - the data is taken directly from a database 225: Some endpoints can have more than 1 data source. (e.g. Memory => Database) This means that the 226: endpoint will check the first Data Source, and if it cannot find the value it's looking for it will 227: check the next one. 228: ## Request Security 229: - Each endpoint has a security type indicating required API key permissions, shown next to the 230: endpoint name (e.g., 231: [New order (TRADE)](rest-api.md#new-order-trade)). 232: - If unspecified, the security type is `NONE`. 233: - Except for `NONE`, all endpoints with a security type are considered `SIGNED` requests (i.e. 234: including a `signature`). 235: - Secure endpoints require a valid API key to be specified and authenticated. 236: - API keys can be created on the 237: [API Management](https://www.binance.com/en/support/faq/360002502072) page of your Binance 238: account. 239: - **Both API key and secret key are sensitive.** Never share them with anyone. If you notice 240: unusual activity in your account, immediately revoke all the keys and contact Binance support. 241: - API keys can be configured to allow access only to certain types of secure endpoints. 242: - For example, you can have an API key with `TRADE` permission for trading, while using a separate 243: API key with `USER_DATA` permission to monitor your order status. 244: - By default, an API key cannot `TRADE`. You need to enable trading in API Management first. 245: | Security type | Description | 246: | ------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | 247: | `NONE` | Public market data | 248: | `TRADE` | Trading on the exchange, placing and canceling orders | 249: | `USER_DATA` | Private account information, such as order status and your trading history | 250: | `USER_STREAM` | Managing User Data Stream subscriptions | 251: ### SIGNED Endpoint security 252: - `SIGNED` endpoints require an additional parameter, `signature`, to be sent in the `query string` 253: or `request body`. 254: #### Signature Case Sensitivity 255: - **HMAC:** Signatures generated using HMAC are **not case-sensitive**. This means the signature 256: string can be verified regardless of letter casing. 257: - **RSA:** Signatures generated using RSA are **case-sensitive**. 258: - **Ed25519:** Signatures generated using Ed25519 are also **case-sensitive** 259: Please consult [SIGNED request example (HMAC)](#hmac-keys), 260: [SIGNED request example (RSA)](#rsa-keys), and [SIGNED request example (Ed25519)](#ed25519-keys) on 261: how to compute signature, depending on which API key type you are using. 262: 263: ### Timing security 264: - `SIGNED` requests also require a `timestamp` parameter which should be the current timestamp 265: either in milliseconds or microseconds. (See [General API Information](#general-api-information)) 266: - An additional optional parameter, `recvWindow`, specifies for how long the request stays valid and 267: may only be specified in milliseconds. 268: - `recvWindow` supports up to three decimal places of precision (e.g., 6000.346) so that 269: microseconds may be specified. 270: - If `recvWindow` is not sent, **it defaults to 5000 milliseconds**. 271: - Maximum `recvWindow` is 60000 milliseconds. 272: - Request processing logic is as follows: 273: ```javascript 274: serverTime = getCurrentTime() 275: if (timestamp < (serverTime + 1 second) && (serverTime - timestamp) <= recvWindow) { 276: // begin processing request 277: serverTime = getCurrentTime() 278: if (serverTime - timestamp) <= recvWindow { 279: // forward request to Matching Engine 280: } else { 281: // reject request 282: } 283: // finish processing request 284: } else { 285: // reject request 286: } 287: ``` 288: **Serious trading is about timing.** Networks can be unstable and unreliable, which can lead to 289: requests taking varying amounts of time to reach the servers. With `recvWindow`, you can specify 290: that the request must be processed within a certain number of milliseconds or be rejected by the 291: server. 292: **It is recommended to use a small recvWindow of 5000 or less! The max cannot go beyond 60,000!** 293: ### SIGNED Endpoint Examples for POST /api/v3/order 294: #### HMAC Keys 295: The signature payload of your request is the query string concatenated without separator to the HTTP 296: body. Any non-ASCII character must be percent-encoded before signing. 297: Here is a step-by-step example of how to send a valid signed payload from the Linux command line 298: using `echo`, `openssl`, and `curl`. There is one example with a symbol name comprised entirely of 299: ASCII characters and one example with a symbol name containing non-ASCII characters. 300: Example API key and secret key: 301: | Key | Value | 302: | ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- | 303: | `apiKey` | vmPUZE6mv9SD5VNHk4HlWFsOr6aKE2zvsw0MuIgwCIPy6utIco14y7Ju91duEh8A | 304: | `secretKey` | NhqPtmdSJYdKjVHjA7PZj4Mge3R5YNiP1e3UZjInClVN65XAbvqqM6A7H5fATj0j | 305: **WARNING: DO NOT SHARE YOUR API KEY AND SECRET KEY WITH ANYONE.** 306: The example keys are provided here only for illustrative purposes. 307: Example of request with a symbol name comprised entirely of ASCII characters: 308: | Parameter | Value | 309: | ------------- | ------------- | 310: | `symbol` | LTCBTC | 311: | `side` | BUY | 312: | `type` | LIMIT | 313: | `timeInForce` | GTC | 314: | `quantity` | 1 | 315: | `price` | 0.1 | 316: | `recvWindow` | 5000 | 317: | `timestamp` | 1499827319559 | 318: Example of a request with a symbol name containing non-ASCII characters: 319: | Parameter | Value | 320: | ------------- | ------------- | 321: | `symbol` | １２３４５６ | 322: | `side` | BUY | 323: | `type` | LIMIT | 324: | `timeInForce` | GTC | 325: | `quantity` | 1 | 326: | `price` | 0.1 | 327: | `recvWindow` | 5000 | 328: | `timestamp` | 1499827319559 | 329: **Step 1: Construct the signature payload** 330: 1. Format parameters as `parameter=value` pairs separated by `&`. 331: 2. Percent-encode the string. 332: For the first set of example parameters (ASCII only), the `parameter=value` string should look like 333: this: 334: ```console 335: symbol=LTCBTC&side=BUY&type=LIMIT&timeInForce=GTC&quantity=1&price=0.1&recvWindow=5000×tamp=1499827319559 336: ``` 337: After percent-encoding, the signature payload should look like this: 338: ```console 339: symbol=LTCBTC&side=BUY&type=LIMIT&timeInForce=GTC&quantity=1&price=0.1&recvWindow=5000×tamp=1499827319559 340: ``` 341: For the second set of example parameters (some non-ASCII characters), the `parameter=value` string 342: should look like this: 343: ```console 344: symbol=１２３４５６&side=BUY&type=LIMIT&timeInForce=GTC&quantity=1&price=0.1&recvWindow=5000×tamp=1499827319559 345: ``` 346: After percent-encoding, the signature payload should look like this: 347: ```console 348: symbol=%EF%BC%91%EF%BC%92%EF%BC%93%EF%BC%94%EF%BC%95%EF%BC%96&side=BUY&type=LIMIT&timeInForce=GTC&quantity=1&price=0.1&recvWindow=5000×tamp=1499827319559 349: ``` 350: **Step 2: Compute the signature** 351: 1. REST API 9: | Production | Testnet | 10: | --------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | 11: | `https://api.binance.com/api` | `https://testnet.binance.vision/api` | 12: | `https://api-gcp.binance.com/api` | `https://api1.testnet.binance.vision/api` | 13: | `https://api1.binance.com/api` | | 14: | `https://api2.binance.com/api` | | 15: | `https://api3.binance.com/api` | | 16: | `https://api4.binance.com/api` | | 17: ## WebSocket API 18: | Production | Testnet | 19: | ----------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | 20: | `wss://ws-api.binance.com/ws-api/v3` | `wss://ws-api.testnet.binance.vision/ws-api/v3` | 21: | `wss://ws-api.binance.com:9443/ws-api/v3` | `wss://ws-api.testnet.binance.vision:9443/ws-api/v3` | 22: ## WebSocket Streams 23: | Type | Production | Testnet | 24: | ---------------- | -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | 25: | Raw streams | `wss://stream.binance.com/ws` | `wss://stream.testnet.binance.vision/stream` | 26: | Raw streams | `wss://stream.binance.com:9443/ws` | `wss://stream.testnet.binance.vision:9443/stream` | 27: | Combined streams | `wss://stream.binance.com/stream` | `wss://stream.testnet.binance.vision/stream` | 28: | Combined streams | `wss://stream.binance.com:9443/stream` | `wss://stream.testnet.binance.vision:9443/stream` | 29: ## FIX Order Entry (OE) 37: | Mode | Production | Testnet | 38: | ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | 39: | Standard | `tcp+tls://fix-oe.binance.com:9000` | `tcp+tls://fix-oe.testnet.binance.vision:9000` | 40: | FIX request / FIX SBE response | `tcp+tls://fix-oe.binance.com:9001` | `tcp+tls://fix-oe.testnet.binance.vision:9001` | 41: | FIX SBE request / FIX SBE response | `tcp+tls://fix-oe.binance.com:9002` | `tcp+tls://fix-oe.testnet.binance.vision:9002` | 42: ##
