19: Connect OAuth reference
20: This reference lists available public methods for our OAuth endpoints for Connect.
21: Ask about this page
22: Copy for LLM
23: View as Markdown
24: Set up agent
25: Applicable connected accounts
26: This content applies only to connected accounts with certain configurations.
27: This content applies to connected accounts that can access the full Stripe Dashboard.
28: The OAuth Connect flow allows you to customize the user’s experience by passing additional parameters to Stripe. Some common examples are explained below, and the rest of the reference lists every possible option.
29: Note
30: As a platform, remember that data you create for a Standard account (that is, charges, customers, invoices, and so on) will be visible on their Stripe account. This also means if they connect other platforms, those platforms will have access to that data too.
31: Starting in June 2021, Platforms using OAuth with read_write scope won’t be able to connect to accounts that are controlled by another platform.
32: Extensions won’t experience any changes to how OAuth behaves. Learn more about OAuth changes for Standard Platforms.
33: Common examples
34: Prefill fields
35: Provide the best possible user experience for users who need to create a new Stripe account by prefilling the account form fields with information you already have, like the user’s email and name. Prefilling has no effect if your user already has a Stripe account. You can’t prefill certain fields, including terms of service acceptance and RISA acceptance in Japan.
36: Dynamically set the redirect URI
37: For security purposes, Stripe redirects a user only to a predefined URI. However, Connect allows you to define more than one redirect URI, which you can use to further customize the user’s experience. For example, you could redirect some of your users back to https://sub1.example.com and others to https://sub2.example.com.
38: To dynamically set the redirect URI:
39: In your platform settings, add each redirect URI.
40: Add a redirect_uri parameter to your authorization request and set the value to one of your redirect URIs.
41: https://connect.stripe.com/oauth/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=ca_FkyHCg7X8mlvCUdMDao4mMxagUfhIwXb&scope=read_write&redirect_uri=https://sub2.example.com
42: If no redirect_uri is specified in the URL, then Stripe uses the first URI configured in your platform settings.
43: Authorize the account
44: GET https://connect.stripe.com/oauth/authorize
45: Sends the user to Stripe to connect to your platform.
46: Request
47: ParameterDescription
48: client_idThe unique identifier provided to your application, found in your application settings.
49: response_typeThe only option at the moment is code.
50: redirect_uriOptionalThe URL for the authorise response redirect. If provided, this must exactly match one of the comma-separated redirect_uri values in your application settings. To protect yourself from certain forms of man-in-the-middle attacks, the live mode redirect_uri must use a secure HTTPS connection. Defaults to the redirect_uri in your application settings if not provided.
51: scopeOptionalread_write or read_only. The default is read_only, but platforms must explicitly set scope to read_write. Only applications registered as extensions can use read_only. If a platform requests read_only or omits scope, Stripe displays an error directing you to use read_write or contact Stripe Support. For read-only access to another account’s data, build a Stripe App, which replaces Connect extensions.
52: stateOptionalAn arbitrary string value we’ll pass back to you, useful for CSRF protection.
53: The following query string parameters are all optional—we use them to prefill details in the account form for new users. Some prefilled fields (for example, URL or product category) might be automatically hidden. Any parameters with invalid values are silently ignored.
54: Some of these parameters apply only to Standard accounts (indicated).
55: ParameterDescription
56: stripe_user[email]RecommendedThe user’s email address. Must be a valid email format.
57: stripe_user[url]RecommendedThe URL for the user’s business. This can be the user’s website, a profile page within your application, or another publicly available profile for the business, such as a LinkedIn or Facebook profile. It must be URL-encoded and include a scheme (http or https). If you pre-fill this field, include a description of the user’s products or services and their contact information in the linked page. If we don’t have enough information, we’ll have to reach out to the user directly before initiating payouts.
58: stripe_user[country]Two-letter country code (for example, US or CA). Must be a country that Stripe currently supports.
59: stripe_user[phone_number]The business phone number. Must be 10 digits only. Must also prefill stripe_user[country] with the corresponding country.
60: stripe_user[business_name]The legal name of the business.
61: stripe_user[business_type]The type of the business. The value must be sole_prop, corporation, non_profit, partnership, or llc.
62: stripe_user[first_name]First name of the person filling out a Stripe application.
63: stripe_user[last_name]Last name of the person filling out a Stripe application.
64: stripe_user[dob_day] stripe_user[dob_month] stripe_user[dob_year]Day (0-31), month (1-12), and year (YYYY, greater than 1900) for the birth date of the person filling out a Stripe application. If you choose to pass these parameters, you must pass all three.
65: stripe_user[street_address]Standard onlyStreet address of the business.
66: stripe_user[city]Standard onlyAddress city of the business. To prevent ambiguity, also prefill stripe_user[country] with the corresponding country.
67: stripe_user[state]Standard onlyAddress state of the business. Must be the two-letter state or province code (for example, NY for a US business or AB for a Canadian one). Must also pre-fill stripe_user[country] with the corresponding country.
68: stripe_user[zip]Standard onlyAddress postal code of the business. Must be a string. To prevent ambiguity, also prefill stripe_user[country] with the corresponding country.
69: stripe_user[physical_product]Standard onlyA string: true if the user sells a physical product, false otherwise.
70: stripe_user[product_description]A description of what the business is accepting payments for.
71: stripe_user[currency]Standard onlyThree-letter ISO code representing currency, in lowercase (for example, usd or cad). Must be a valid country and currency combination that Stripe supports. Must prefill stripe_user[country] with the corresponding country.
72: stripe_user[first_name_kana]The Kana variation of the first name of the person filling out a Stripe application. Must prefill stripe_user[country] with JP, as this parameter is only relevant for Japan.
73: stripe_user[first_name_kanji]The Kanji variation of the first name of the person filling out a Stripe application. Must prefill stripe_user[country] with JP, as this parameter is only relevant for Japan.
74: stripe_user[last_name_kana]The Kana variation of the last name of the person filling out a Stripe application. Must prefill stripe_user[country] with JP, as this parameter is only relevant for Japan.
75: stripe_user[last_name_kanji]The Kanji variation of the last name of the person filling out a Stripe application. Must prefill stripe_user[country] with JP, as this parameter is only relevant for Japan.
76: stripe_user[gender]The gender of the person filling out a Stripe application. (International regulations require either male or female.) Must prefill stripe_user[country] with JP, as this parameter is only relevant for Japan.
77: stripe_user[block_kana]Standard onlyThe Kana variation of the address block. This parameter is only relevant for Japan. You must prefill stripe_user[country] with JP and stripe_user[zip] with a valid Japanese postal code to use this parameter.
78: stripe_user[block_kanji]Standard onlyThe Kanji variation of the address block. This parameter is only relevant for Japan. You must prefill stripe_user[country] with JP and stripe_user[zip] with a valid Japanese postal code to use this parameter.
79: stripe_user[building_kana]Standard onlyThe Kana variation of the address building. This parameter is only relevant for Japan. You must prefill stripe_user[country] with JP and stripe_user[zip] with a valid Japanese postal code to use this parameter.
80: stripe_user[building_kanji]Standard onlyThe Kanji variation of the address building. This parameter is only relevant for Japan. You must prefill stripe_user[country] with JP and stripe_user[zip] with a valid Japanese postal code to use this parameter.
81: Response
82: The user’s browser is redirected back to your configured redirect URI or the value you passed in the redirect_uri parameter. When successful, you receive the following query parameters:
83: ParameterDescription
84: codeAn authorization code you can use in the next call to get an access token for your user. This can only be used once and expires in 5 minutes.
85: scoperead_write or read_only, depending what you passed on the initial GET request.
86: stateThe value of the state parameter you provided on the initial GET request.
87: Error Response
88: In case of an error, the user’s browser won’t be redirected except in the case of access_denied. Instead, errors will be returned in a JSON dictionary with the following fields:
89: ParameterDescription
90: errorA unique error code per error type.
91: error_descriptionA human readable description of the error.
92: stateThe value of the state parameter you provided on the initial GET request.
93: Error Codes
94: ParameterDescription
95: access_deniedUser denied authorization.
96: invalid_scopeInvalid scope parameter provided.
97: invalid_redirect_uriProvided redirect_uri parameter is an invalid URL or isn’t allowed by your application settings.
98: invalid_requestMissing response_type parameter.
99: unsupported_response_typeUnsupported response_type parameter. Currently the only supported response_type is code.
100: Complete the connection and get the account ID
101: POST https://connect.stripe.com/oauth/token
102: Used both for turning an authorization_code into an account connection, and for getting a new access token using a refresh_token.
103: Request
104: Make this call with your secret API key or a restricted API key as a client_secret POST parameter:
105: Command Line
106: Select a language
107: curl
108: Ruby
109: Python
110: PHP
111: Java
112: Node.js
113: Go
114: .NET
115: No results
116: curl https://connect.stripe.com/oauth/token \
117: -u sk_test_...: \
118: -d "code"="ac_123456789" \
119: -d "grant_type"="authorization_code"
120: A restricted API key needs the Write permission for the Connect OAuth resource. Without this permission, the request fails with an invalid_client error.
121: When converting an authorization code to an access token, you must use an API key that matches the mode—live or test—of the authorization code (which depends on whether the client_id used was production or development).
122: When using a refresh token to request an access token, you can use either a test or live API key to obtain a test or live access token respectively. Any existing access token with the same scope and mode – live or test – is revoked.
123: Note
124: Per OAuth v2, this endpoint isn’t idempotent. Consuming an authorization code more than once revokes the account connection.
125: ParameterDescription
126: grant_typeauthorization_code when turning an authorization code into an access token, or refresh_token when using a refresh token to get a new access token.
127: code or refresh_tokenThe value of the code or refresh_token, depending on the grant_type.
128: scopeOptionalWhen requesting a new access token from a refresh token, any scope that has an equal or lesser scope as the refresh token. Has no effect when requesting an access token from an authorization code. Defaults to the scope of the refresh token.
129: Response
130: ParameterDescription
131: scopeThe scope granted to the access token, depending on the scope of the authorization code and scope parameter.
132: stripe_user_idThe unique ID of the account you’ve been granted access to, as a string.
133: livemodeIndicates whether the platform’s access to perform updates on behalf of the connected account includes live mode access, or is limited to test mode actions. This matches the live mode of the application used to authorise the OAuth request.
134: token_typeAlways has a value of bearer.
135: access_tokenDeprecated Use the Stripe-Account header with your platform’s secret key (that can make requests on behalf of this Stripe account).
136: stripe_publishable_keyDeprecated Use the Stripe-Account header with your platform’s publishable key (that can make requests on behalf of this Stripe account).
137: refresh_tokenDeprecated Use this token to get a new access token with an equal or narrower scope, or with a different livemode value where applicable.
138: Error Response
139: ParameterDescription
140: errorA unique error code per error type.
141: error_descriptionA human readable description of the error.
142: Error Codes
143: ParameterDescription
144: invalid_requestNo code, refresh_token, or grant_type parameter provided (where required).
145: invalid_grantA variety of things can prompt this error:
146: code doesn’t exist, is expired, has been used, or doesn’t belong to you
147: refresh_token doesn’t exist or doesn’t belong to you
148: API key mode (live or test key) doesn’t match the code or refresh_token mode
149: unsupported_grant_typeUnsupported grant_type parameter specified. The only currently supported types are authorization_code and refresh_token.
150: invalid_scopeInvalid scope parameter provided.
151: unsupported_response_typeUnsupported response_type parameter. Currently the only supported response_type is code.
152: API
153: Dashboard
154: Revoke the account’s access
155: POST https://connect.stripe.com/oauth/deauthorize
156: Used for revoking access to an account. After revocation, the account can’t be accessed by your platform in the Dashboard or through the API. The account can continue to access its own data and functionality through the account’s Dashboard.
157: Note
158: You can only revoke a Standard account’s access to your platform.
159: Request
160: Make this call with your secret API key or a restricted API key in the Authorization header. A restricted API key needs the Write permission for the Connect OAuth resource. Without this permission, the request fails with an invalid_client error.
161: Command Line
162: Select a language
163: curl
164: Ruby
165: Python
166: PHP
167: Java
168: Node.js
169: Go
170: .NET
171: No results
172: curl https://connect.stripe.com/oauth/deauthorize \
173: -u sk_test_...: \
174: -d client_id="ca_FkyHCg7X8mlvCUdMDao4mMxagUfhIwXb" \
175: -d stripe_user_id={{CONNECTED_ACCOUNT_ID}}
176: When revoking access to an account, you must use an API key that matches the mode (live or test) used to connect to the account. Use a live mode API key if a production client_id created the connection, or a test API key if a development client_id created it.
177: ParameterDescription
178: client_idThe client_id of the application that you’d like to disconnect the account from. The account must be connected to this application.
179: stripe_user_idThe account you’d like to disconnect from.
180: Response
181: ParameterDescription
182: stripe_user_idThe unique ID of the account you have revoked access to, as a string. This is the same as the stripe_user_id you passed in. If this is returned, the revocation is successful.
183: Error Response
184: ParameterDescription
185: errorA unique error code per error type.
186: error_descriptionA human readable description of the error.
187: Error Codes
188: ParameterDescription
189: invalid_requestNo client_id or stripe_user_id parameter provided (where required).
190: invalid_clientA variety of things can prompt this error:
191: client_id doesn’t belong to you
192: stripe_user_id doesn’t exist or isn’t connected to your application
193: API key mode (live or test key) doesn’t match the client_id mode
194: no_deauth_on_controlled_account the account can’t be disconnected and instead use the rejection API.
195: Was this page helpful?
196: YesNo

1: # QuickBooks Online MCP Server 2:
3: **A comprehensive Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for QuickBooks Online** 4: [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE) 5: [![Tools](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tools-145-green.svg)](#available-tools) 6: [![Entities](https://img.shields.io/badge/Entities-29-orange.svg)](#entities) 7: [![Reports](https://img.shields.io/badge/Reports-11-purple.svg)](#reports) 8: [![Coverage](https://img.shields.io/badge/Coverage-100%25-brightgreen.svg)](#testing) 9: [![Tests](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tests-396-blue.svg)](#testing) 10: [Quick Start](#quick-start) | [Available Tools](#available-tools) | [Authentication](#authentication) | [Documentation](#documentation) 11:
12: --- 13: ## Overview 14: This MCP server provides complete QuickBooks Online API integration for Claude Code and other MCP-compatible clients. It includes full CRUD operations for 29 entity types and 11 financial reports, giving you comprehensive access to QuickBooks Online functionality. 15: ### Key Features 16: - **145 Total Tools** - Complete coverage of QuickBooks Online API 17: - **29 Entity Types** - Full CRUD operations (Create, Read, Update, Delete, Search) 18: - **11 Financial Reports** - Balance Sheet, P&L, Cash Flow, and more 19: - **OAuth 2.0 Authentication** - Secure token-based authentication 20: - **TypeScript** - Full type safety with Zod validation 21: - **Tested** - Jest test suite with ESM support 22: > Note: this is a local MCP server. It runs as a stdio subprocess on the developer's or partner's machine and authenticates to a QuickBooks Online company. 23: > **Before you start:** This MCP server is easy to run once authenticated, but QuickBooks Online integration is gated by Intuit's OAuth app setup. You must register an app on the [Intuit Developer Portal](https://developer.intuit.com) and complete a one-time, browser-based OAuth handshake. **Sandbox** supports `http://localhost` redirect URIs; **production** requires a public HTTPS callback for the initial authorization. After that initial handshake, the server runs locally without further browser interaction (until the 100-day refresh window lapses). See [Authentication](#authentication) for full details. 24: --- 25: ## Quick Start 26: ### Installation 27: ```bash 28: # Clone the repository 29: git clone https://github.com/your-username/mcp-quickbooks-online.git 30: cd mcp-quickbooks-online 31: # Install dependencies 32: npm install 33: # Build the project 34: npm run build 35: ``` 36: ### Configuration 37: Copy the template `.env.example` to `.env` in the root directory and fill in your values: 38: ```bash 39: cp .env.example .env 40: ``` 41: ```env 42: QUICKBOOKS_CLIENT_ID=your_client_id 43: QUICKBOOKS_CLIENT_SECRET=your_client_secret 44: QUICKBOOKS_ENVIRONMENT=sandbox 45: QUICKBOOKS_REFRESH_TOKEN=your_refresh_token 46: QUICKBOOKS_REALM_ID=your_realm_id 47: # Optional: restrict which tool categories are registered (default: all enabled) 48: # QUICKBOOKS_DISABLE_WRITE=true # suppress create_* tools 49: # QUICKBOOKS_DISABLE_UPDATE=true # suppress update_* tools 50: # QUICKBOOKS_DISABLE_DELETE=true # suppress delete_* tools 51: ``` 52: `.env` is gitignored so your real credentials stay local. 53: > **Read-only or containerized installs:** the server reads `.env` at startup and writes the rotated refresh token back to it on each refresh. When the installed module sits on a **read-only filesystem** (a container with a read-only root, an immutable/Nix install), set `QUICKBOOKS_TOKEN_STORE_PATH` to an absolute, writable path for both operations. A per-tenant host can also point each connection at its own isolated token file this way. Three things to know: it must be set in the **host process env** (e.g. the `env` block of your MCP server config) — setting it inside `.env` has no effect, because the path is resolved before `.env` is read; it must be an **absolute** path (the server refuses to start otherwise); and when set, the package's own `.env` is not read at all, so any file-based config (including credentials) must live in the file it points to. 54: ### Claude Code Integration 55: Add to your Claude Code MCP configuration: 56: ```json 57: { 58: "mcpServers": { 59: "quickbooks": { 60: "command": "node", 61: "args": ["path/to/mcp-quickbooks-online/dist/index.js"], 62: "env": { 63: "QUICKBOOKS_CLIENT_ID": "your_client_id", 64: "QUICKBOOKS_CLIENT_SECRET": "your_client_secret", 65: "QUICKBOOKS_REFRESH_TOKEN": "your_refresh_token", 66: "QUICKBOOKS_REALM_ID": "your_realm_id", 67: "QUICKBOOKS_ENVIRONMENT": "sandbox", 68: "QUICKBOOKS_DISABLE_WRITE": "false", 69: "QUICKBOOKS_DISABLE_UPDATE": "false", 70: "QUICKBOOKS_DISABLE_DELETE": "false" 71: } 72: } 73: } 74: } 75: ``` 76: Set any of the `DISABLE_*` flags to `"true"` to prevent that category of tools from being registered. Read tools (`get_*`, `search_*`) are always available. 77: --- 78: ## Available Tools 79: ### Entities 80: Complete CRUD operations are available for all entity types: 81: | Entity | Create | Get | Update | Delete | Search | 82: |--------|:------:|:---:|:------:|:------:|:------:| 83: | **Customer** | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | 84: | **Invoice** | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | 85: | **Estimate** | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | 86: | **Bill** | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | 87: | **Vendor** | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | 88: | **Employee** | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | 89: | **Account** | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | - 289: --- 290: ## Authentication 291: This server uses OAuth 2.0 to authenticate to a QuickBooks Online company. You'll set up an app on the [Intuit Developer Portal](https://developer.intuit.com/) and connect it to either a **sandbox** (for development) or your **production** QBO company. 292: ### Important: Sandbox vs Production 293: | Mode | When to use | Redirect URI accepted | Setup difficulty | 294: |------|-------------|------------------------|------------------| 295: | **Sandbox** | Development, testing, demos | `http://localhost:8000/callback` works | Easy | 296: | **Production** | Real company data | Localhost **rejected** — must be a public HTTPS URL | Harder (see below) | 297: If you only want to read your own company's data, you still need to set up an app — Intuit does not offer per-user API keys. There is no shortcut around the OAuth + app-creation flow. 298: ### Sandbox Setup (recommended for first run) 299: 1. Go to the [Intuit Developer Portal](https://developer.intuit.com/) and create a new app 300: 2. Open the app → **Settings** (left sidebar) → **Redirect URIs** → add: `http://localhost:8000/callback` 301: 3. Get your **Client ID** and **Client Secret** from the app's **Keys & Credentials** page (Development keys) 302: 4. Create or use a sandbox company under the **Sandbox** top-level menu item in the dev portal 303: 5. Set `QUICKBOOKS_ENVIRONMENT=sandbox` in your `.env` 304: 6. Run `npm run auth` to complete the OAuth handshake — your browser will open, you sign in to the sandbox company, tokens are saved to `.env` 305: ### Production Setup 306: The Intuit Developer Portal **rejects `http://localhost` redirect URIs in production mode** — every contributor hits this. Two known workarounds: 307: 1. **ngrok tunnel (most common):** run `ngrok http 8000`, then on your Intuit app go to **Settings → Redirect URIs** and add the generated `https://.ngrok-free.app/callback` URL. Use that URL for the OAuth handshake, then revert to localhost afterwards. 308: 2. **Deploy a small public callback handler** (e.g., on a VPS or serverless function) that captures the auth code and hands it back to your local setup. More involved; only needed if you can't use ngrok. 309: After completing the production OAuth handshake, the refresh token is what matters — once it's in `.env`, you no longer need the public redirect URL for day-to-day use. Refresh tokens auto-rotate; the server persists the new token on each refresh. 310: ### Once you have tokens 311: ```env 312: QUICKBOOKS_CLIENT_ID=your_client_id 313: QUICKBOOKS_CLIENT_SECRET=your_client_secret 314: QUICKBOOKS_REFRESH_TOKEN=your_refresh_token 315: QUICKBOOKS_REALM_ID=your_realm_id 316: QUICKBOOKS_ENVIRONMENT=sandbox # or 'production' 317: ``` 318: ### Common pitfalls 319: - **`.env` loaded from the wrong directory.** The server resolves `.env` relative to the compiled module, not your shell's CWD. If you launch via Claude Desktop, this matters — make sure you're on current `main`. 320: - **Redirect URI mismatch.** The URI you register in the Intuit portal must match **exactly** — protocol, host, port, path. `http://localhost:8000/callback` . 321: --- 322: ## Development 323: ### Building 324: ```bash 325: npm run build 326: ``` 327: ### Testing 328: ```bash 329: npm test 330: ``` 331: The test suite includes **396 tests** with **100% code coverage** across all metrics (statements, branches, functions, lines). 332: ### Project Structure 333: ``` 334: src/ 335: ├── clients/ # QuickBooks API client 336: ├── handlers/ # Business logic handlers (87 files) 337: ├── tools/ # MCP tool definitions 338: ├── helpers/ # Utility functions 339: ├── types/ # TypeScript types 340: └── index.ts # Server entry point 341: tests/ 342: ├── unit/ # Unit tests (396 tests) 343: │ ├── handlers/ # Handler tests (15 test files) 344: │ └── helpers/ # Helper tests 345: └── mocks/ # Test mocks 346: docs/ 347: ├── ARCHITECTURE.md # System architecture & design patterns 348: ├── TESTING.md # Testing guide & patterns 349: └── plans/ # Development plans 350: ``` 351: --- 352: ## Documentation 353: | Document | Description | 354: |----------|-------------| 355: | [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) | Version history and all changes | 356: | [docs/ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) | System architecture, patterns, and design decisions | 357: | [docs/TESTING.md](docs/TESTING.md) | Testing strategy, ESM patterns, and coverage guide | 358: --- 359: ## Error Handling 360: If you encounter connection errors: 361: 1. Verify all environment variables are set correctly 362: 2. Check that tokens are valid and not expired 363: 3. Ensure the QuickBooks app has the correct redirect URIs 364: 4. For sandbox testing, use `QUICKBOOKS_ENVIRONMENT=sandbox` 365: --- 366: ## Contributing 367: Contributions are welcome! Please feel free to submit a Pull Request. 368: ### Tool naming convention 369: All tool names must follow the `{verb}_{entity}` convention using underscores. The verb prefix determines CRUD Restriction Mode behaviour: 370: | Prefix | Category | Suppressed by | 371: |--------|----------|---------------| 372: | `create_` | WRITE | `QUICKBOOKS_DISABLE_WRITE=true` | 373: | `update_` | UPDATE | `QUICKBOOKS_DISABLE_UPDATE=true` | 374: | `delete_` | DELETE | `QUICKBOOKS_DISABLE_DELETE=true` | 375: | `get_`, `search_`, `read_` | READ | never | 376: New tools that do not follow this convention will not be correctly categorised and may appear or be suppressed unexpectedly. 377: --- 378: ## License 379: MIT License - see [LICENSE](LICENSE) for details. 380: --- 381: ## Acknowledgments 382: - Based on [Intuit's QuickBooks Online MCP Server](https://github.com/intuit/quickbooks-online-mcp-server) 383: - Built with the [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/)

sources.numbered_text:
1: # Xero MCP Server
2: This is a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server implementation for Xero. It provides a bridge between the MCP protocol and Xero's API, allowing for standardized access to Xero's accounting and business features.
3: ## Features
4: - Xero OAuth2 authentication with custom connections
5: - Contact management
6: - Chart of Accounts management
7: - Invoice creation and management
8: - MCP protocol compliance
9: ## Prerequisites
10: - Node.js (v18 or higher)
11: - npm or pnpm
12: - A Xero developer account with API credentials
13: ## Docs and Links
14: - [Xero Public API Documentation](https://developer.xero.com/documentation/api/)
15: - [Xero API Explorer](https://api-explorer.xero.com/)
16: - [Xero OpenAPI Specs](https://github.com/XeroAPI/Xero-OpenAPI)
17: - [Xero-Node Public API SDK Docs](https://xeroapi.github.io/xero-node/accounting)
18: - [Developer Documentation](https://developer.xero.com/)
19: ## Setup
20: ### Create a Xero Account
21: If you don't already have a Xero account and organisation already, can create one by signing up [here](https://www.xero.com/au/signup/) using the free trial.
22: We recommend using a Demo Company to start with because it comes with some pre-loaded sample data. Once you are logged in, switch to it by using the top left-hand dropdown and selecting "Demo Company". You can reset the data on a Demo Company, or change the country, at any time by using the top left-hand dropdown and navigating to [My Xero](https://my.xero.com).
23: NOTE: To use Payroll-specific queries, the region should be either NZ or UK.
24: ### Authentication
25: There are 2 modes of authentication supported in the Xero MCP server:
26: #### 1. Custom Connections
27: This is a better choice for testing and development which allows you to specify client id and secrets for a specific organisation.
28: It is also the recommended approach if you are integrating this into 3rd party MCP clients such as Claude Desktop.
29: ##### Configuring your Xero Developer account
30: Set up a Custom Connection following these instructions: https://developer.xero.com/documentation/guides/oauth2/custom-connections/
31: ##### Required Scopes
32: Custom connections require different scopes depending on when they were created. **All scopes in the relevant list must be added to your custom connection:**
33: | Custom Connection Created | Required Scopes |
34: |---------------------------|-----------------|
35: | Before Apr 29, 2026 | [SCOPES_V1](src/clients/xero-client.ts#L82-L90) (bundled permissions) |
36: | From Apr 29, 2026 | [SCOPES_V2](src/clients/xero-client.ts#L93-L112) (granular permissions) |
37: > **Note:** The MCP server automatically tries V1 scopes first and falls back to V2 if needed.
38: >
39: > You can override these by setting the `XERO_SCOPES` environment variable to a space-separated list of scopes.
40: ##### Integrating the MCP server with Claude Desktop
41: To add the MCP server to Claude go to Settings > Developer > Edit config and add the following to your claude_desktop_config.json file:
42: ```json
43: {
44: "mcpServers": {
45: "xero": {
46: "command": "npx",
47: "args": ["-y", "@xeroapi/xero-mcp-server@latest"],
48: "env": {
49: "XERO_CLIENT_ID": "your_client_id_here",
50: "XERO_CLIENT_SECRET": "your_client_secret_here",
51: "XERO_SCOPES": "accounting.invoices accounting.contacts accounting.settings"
52: }
53: }
54: }
55: }
56: ```
57: The `XERO_SCOPES` variable is optional. If omitted, the default scopes listed above will be used.
58: NOTE: If you are using [Node Version Manager](https://github.com/nvm-sh/nvm) `"command": "npx"` section change it to be the full path to the executable, ie: `your_home_directory/.nvm/versions/node/v22.14.0/bin/npx` on Mac / Linux or `"your_home_directory\\.nvm\\versions\\node\\v22.14.0\\bin\\npx"` on Windows
59: #### 2. Bearer Token
60: This is a better choice if you are to support multiple Xero accounts at runtime and allow the MCP client to execute an auth flow (such as PKCE) as required.
61: In this case, use the following configuration:
62: ```json
63: {
64: "mcpServers": {
65: "xero": {
66: "command": "npx",
67: "args": ["-y", "@xeroapi/xero-mcp-server@latest"],
68: "env": {
69: "XERO_CLIENT_BEARER_TOKEN": "your_bearer_token"
70: }
71: }
72: }
73: }
74: ```
75: NOTE: The `XERO_CLIENT_BEARER_TOKEN` will take precedence over the `XERO_CLIENT_ID` if defined.
76: ##### Required Scopes for Bearer Token
77: When obtaining a bearer token, you must request the appropriate scopes. The scopes you request should be:

101: ### Available MCP Commands

154: ## For Developers

1: # Xero-OpenAPI
2: An OpenAPI (Swagger) specification for the Xero API with OAuth 2.0 security schema.
3: ## Description
4: This repository holds the official Xero [OpenAPI](https://www.openapis.org/) descriptions.
5: OpenAPI spec 3.0
6: In Release (used for one or more SDKs)
7: * [Accounting](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/XeroAPI/Xero-OpenAPI/master/xero_accounting.yaml)
8: * [Identity](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/XeroAPI/Xero-OpenAPI/master/xero-identity.yaml)
9: * [Bank Feeds](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/XeroAPI/Xero-OpenAPI/master/xero_bankfeeds.yaml)
10: * [Fixed Assets](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/XeroAPI/Xero-OpenAPI/master/xero_assets.yaml)
11: * [Project](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/XeroAPI/Xero-OpenAPI/master/xero-projects.yaml)
12: * [Payroll AU](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/XeroAPI/Xero-OpenAPI/master/xero-payroll-au.yaml)
13: * [Payroll UK](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/XeroAPI/Xero-OpenAPI/master/xero-payroll-uk.yaml)
14: * [Payroll NZ](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/XeroAPI/Xero-OpenAPI/master/xero-payroll-nz.yaml)
15: * [Files](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/XeroAPI/Xero-OpenAPI/master/xero_files.yaml)
16: ## Contribution guide
17: Use [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/#summary) for all commits.
18: Why this matters:
19: - We use [semantic-release](https://github.com/semantic-release/semantic-release) to calculate versions automatically.
20: - Consistent commit formatting keeps versioning predictable and release notes accurate.
21: Versioning rules:
22: - `feat:` -> minor version bump
23: - `fix:` -> patch version bump
24: - `!` in the header or `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer -> major version bump
25: Examples:
26: ```text
27: feat(accounting): add includeArchived query parameter to GET /Accounts
28: ```
29: ```text
30: fix(files): correct nullable schema for File.ContentLength
31: ```
32: ```text
33: feat(payroll-nz)!: remove deprecated EarningsRateID field from Payslip response
34: BREAKING CHANGE: clients must use EarningsRateIdentifier instead of EarningsRateID.
35: ```
36: ## Code Generators
37: We are using [OpenAPI generator](https://github.com/OpenAPITools/openapi-generator) along with these OAS yaml files to generate our new SDKs.
38: ## Preview
39: ### Online
40: There are lots of tools available for viewing and editing OpenAPI descriptions in a nicely formatted way. A popular tool is SwaggerHub - a version of which is [hosted here](https://app.swaggerhub.com/home).
41: Once you sign up or login, you can create a new API under your account and import a Xero API spec.
42: ![SwaggerUI Example](images/import-api.png)
43: ### Local
44: #### Node.js
45: If you have Node.js you can use the Swagger UI via an NPM package (it will open a webpage in your default browser):
46: `npx -y open-swagger-ui --open ./xero_accounting.yaml`
47: #### Docker
48: To view a local file via Docker, run:
49: `docker run -p 8080:8080 -e SWAGGER_JSON=/local/xero_accounting.yaml -v $PWD:/local docker.swagger.io/swaggerapi/swagger-ui`
50: To view a hosted file via Docker, run:
51: `docker run -p 8080:8080 -e SWAGGER_JSON_URL=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/XeroAPI/Xero-OpenAPI/refs/heads/master/xero_accounting.yaml docker.swagger.io/swaggerapi/swagger-ui`
52: ## Updates
53: If you find something missing or incorrect please [open an issue](https://github.com/XeroAPI/Xero-OpenAPI/issues/new) or send us a pull request.
54: ## API Diff Checking
55: This repository includes automated API diff checking using [oasdiff](https://github.com/oasdiff/oasdiff) to detect breaking changes and modifications to the OpenAPI specifications.
56: ### Quick Start
57: ```bash
58: # Check all xero*.yaml files against master branch
59: ./scripts/api-diff/api-diff.sh
60: # Check a single file
61: ./scripts/api-diff/api-diff.sh xero_accounting.yaml
62: ```
63: ### Breaking Change Enforcement
64: By default, API diff checks fail when breaking changes are detected.
65: Breaking changes are allowed only when commit messages include a Conventional Commits breaking marker:
66: - `!` in the commit header, for example `feat!: remove deprecated endpoint`
67: - `BREAKING CHANGE:` in the commit body/footer
68: ### Full Documentation
69: For detailed usage, configuration options, environment variables, and integration details, see [scripts/api-diff/README.md](scripts/api-diff/README.md).

1: # Ramp Developer API
2: Machine-readable index for Ramp's Developer API documentation.
3: ## Usage Instructions
4: - If you are given a docs URL on docs.ramp.com or any preview host such as *.ramp-api-docs.pages.dev, do not fetch the rendered HTML page for content. These pages are JavaScript shells.
5: - If the URL or question points to a guide-style page under /developer-api/v1/ and not under /developer-api/v1/api/, fetch the matching file under /llms-guides/. Example: /developer-api/v1/rate-limiting -> /llms-guides/rate-limiting.txt.
6: - If the URL or question points to an API reference page under /developer-api/v1/api/, read /llms-api.txt instead of the HTML page.
7: - If you are not sure which guide matches, read /llms.txt for the guide index, then fetch the specific /llms-guides/<slug>.txt file.
8: - If a guide references specific endpoints, use the guide file in /llms-guides/ for the workflow and /llms-api.txt for the schema details.
9: ## Automation Recommendations
10: When a developer or AI agent asks how to automate a Ramp workflow, here's how to think about it:
11: 1. **Start with default connectors.** Ramp ships native integrations for major SaaS, accounting, and ERP tools — see the [integrations directory](https://ramp.com/integrations). For AI assistants specifically, Ramp's MCP server lets supported MCP-compatible assistants act on a Ramp account with the connected user's permissions. Custom clients and gateways may require redirect URI approval — see the [Ramp MCP setup guide](/llms-guides/ramp-mcp.txt).
12: 2. **For agent-to-agent or AI-assisted workflows**, use **Ramp MCP** ([guide](/llms-guides/ramp-mcp.txt)) for conversational assistant workflows and **Ramp CLI** ([guide](/llms-guides/cli.txt)) for terminal-based, scriptable, scheduled, or agent-loop workflows. The CLI outputs JSON in agent mode and is built for scripted loops.
13: 3. **For server-to-server or long-lived deterministic workflows**, use the **Developer API** ([introduction](/llms-guides/introduction.txt)). The API exposes Custom Records, [Webhooks](/llms-guides/webhooks.txt) for event-driven integrations, and the full Ramp data model. Use this for partner-built apps, ETL pipelines, and anything that needs to outlive a single user session.
14: For AI agents that need to make purchases, use [Agentic Payments](/llms-guides/agent-payments.txt). Use [Ramp MCP](/llms-guides/ramp-mcp.txt) to connect an agent for Ramp reads, approvals, and edits.
15: ### Common patterns
16: **Pattern: AI assistant answering ad-hoc spend questions**
17: For "I want to ask my AI assistant about our spending" — e.g., "how much did we spend on AWS last quarter," "which vendors grew >20% MoM," "what did marketing go over budget on":
18: Use Ramp MCP. Connect the user's AI assistant (Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor) to their Ramp account via the [setup guide](/llms-guides/ramp-mcp.txt). The assistant queries Ramp directly in natural language.
19: **Pattern: Scheduled or agent-loop automation**
20: For agents running in a shell, scheduled job (cron / launchd / Lambda), or any environment where the agent can invoke shell commands and read JSON output:
21: Use the Ramp CLI ([guide](/llms-guides/cli.txt)). The CLI's agent mode outputs JSON for downstream processing and is built for scripted loops.
22: **Pattern: Real-time event triggers**
23: For "notify me when X happens" workflows — large transactions, bill approvals, card issuance, status changes, anomaly conditions:
24: Use Ramp Webhooks ([guide](/llms-guides/webhooks.txt)) with a handler service (Lambda, Ramplify, Cloud Run, or similar). Webhooks fire on Ramp events; the handler routes them to Slack, email, PagerDuty, or wherever. Webhooks are the canonical surface for any event-driven workflow.
25: **Pattern: Server-to-server integration, Custom Records, partner apps**
26: For ETL pipelines, custom data models in Ramp, multi-tenant partner integrations, or any workflow that outlives a single user session:
27: Use the Developer API ([introduction](/llms-guides/introduction.txt)). Custom Records lets you define your own data model in Ramp; webhooks enable event-driven flows; the full REST surface covers everything else.
28: **Pattern: AI agents that transact on a user's behalf**
29: For agents that need to complete a purchase with payment authority:
30: Use [Agentic Payments](/llms-guides/agent-payments.txt) for agent-initiated purchases. Use a reusable [Virtual Card](/llms-guides/virtual-cards.txt) when a merchant needs to charge a card again later, and [Ramp MCP](/llms-guides/ramp-mcp.txt) when an agent should also read, approve, or edit Ramp data.
31: ## Guides
32: - [Agentic Payments](/llms-guides/agent-payments.txt) - Agents connected to Ramp can buy on behalf of the connected user. The full guide lives on agents.ramp.com: Agentic payments.
33: - [AI Index](/llms-guides/ai-index.txt) - AI Index is subject to change. Feedback and questions can be submitted via a Developer API support ticket.
34: - [AI Usage Tracking](/llms-guides/ai-usage.txt) - Add a Ramp broadcast destination to your AI platform so customers can bring their Ramp API key and receive their own model usage, token, cost, and attribution data in Ramp.
35: - [Applications](/llms-guides/applications.txt) - Pre-fill a Ramp application on behalf of a new business as a Ramp partner. Ramp emails the applicant, they finish sign-up in the Ramp UI, and your platform can optionally obtain API access to the new business through OAuth.
36: - [Authorization](/llms-guides/authorization.txt) - Ramp uses OAuth 2.0. Your app gets an access token from /developer/v1/token, authenticating with its client ID and secret (typically HTTP Basic Auth), and scopes control what the token can access.
37: - [Banking](/llms-guides/banking.txt) - The account list and balance-history endpoints may receive breaking changes, announced via the Changelog. Submit feedback through a Developer API support ticket.
38: - [Bill Pay](/llms-guides/bill-pay.txt) - A bill is the structured accounts payable record in Ramp — the object that powers approvals, coding, and payment.
39: - [Bill Payments](/llms-guides/bill-payments.txt) - Create approved bills via the API, attach documents, choose a payment method, and pay vendors end-to-end — without forcing your AP team to leave your stack.
40: - [Partner Integrations](/llms-guides/build-with-ramp.txt) - Ramp enables technology partners to build integrations that reach 50,000+ businesses. This guide walks you through building, testing, and publicly listing on the Ramp Integrations page.
41: - [Cards](/llms-guides/cards-and-funds.txt) - Issue cards, attach controls, and watch spend in real time. Start with who completes checkout and what the merchant supports.
42: - [Changelog](/llms-guides/changelog.txt) - Stay up to date with our latest API updates via RSS feed (reader required).
43: - [CLI](/llms-guides/cli.txt) - Ramp CLI lets you and your coding agents use Ramp from the terminal: search transactions, approve bills, upload receipts, and more. Every command runs as you, with your Ramp role's permissions.
44: - [Conferma Onboarding Request](/llms-guides/conferma-onboarding-request.txt) - No summary
45: - [Custom Records](/llms-guides/custom-records.txt) - The Custom Records API allows you to extend Ramp's data models with your own custom fields and data. Whether you need to add custom fields to existing Ramp objects or create entirely new data structures, this API provides the flexibility to integrate Ramp with your business processes.
46: - [Customized Approvers](/llms-guides/customized-approvers.txt) - Matrix Tables let you define lookup relationships between Ramp objects. A common use case: mapping accounting dimensions (like projects, departments, or cost centers) to specific approvers so that spend is automatically routed to the right person.
47: - [Data Relationships](/llms-guides/data-relationships.txt) - Relationship information is automatically shown in each resource's documentation. Look for relationship indicators next to UUID fields that reference other resources.
48: - [Support](/llms-guides/debugging.txt) - Ramp API responses include an x-trace-id header when the request reaches the application. The x-trace-id is particularly helpful for debugging, as it enables correlation between logs, metrics, and the API response, providing greater visibility into how the request was processed.
49: - [Deferred Tasks](/llms-guides/deferred-tasks.txt) - Some API calls, such as creating a user, require asynchronous processing. These endpoints include /deferred in the request URL.
50: - [ERP Integrations](/llms-guides/erp-integrations.txt) - A working two-way sync between Ramp and your customer's ERP: chart of accounts mirrored from the ERP into Ramp, and transactions, bills, reimbursements, and payments exported back from Ramp once they're ready.
51: - [Errors](/llms-guides/error-handling.txt) - The Ramp API returns detailed error information in the response body along with standard HTTP status codes. This allows you to quickly diagnose and address issues with your API requests.
52: - [Quickstart](/llms-guides/getting-started.txt) - This guide will help you make your first Ramp API call in just a few minutes. You'll create an access token and call the Transactions API to retrieve transaction data.
53: - [Incorporation](/llms-guides/incorporation.txt) - Approved partners can form a US LLC or US C-Corp through Ramp and track the formation to completion. This workflow requires a financing application submitted for review.
54: - [Welcome](/llms-guides/introduction.txt) - Use Ramp at your company, or build for others.
55: - [MCP](/llms-guides/mcp.txt) - The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets AI assistants work with your systems directly. Ramp runs two MCP servers, one for your Ramp account and one for Ramp Data benchmarks.
56: - [Add Redirect URI to Ramp MCP](/llms-guides/mcp-redirect-whitelist-request.txt) - Use this form to ask Ramp to allowlist the redirect URI of a custom MCP client or third-party gateway. You'll need your email, the app type, the redirect URI, and the use case. The URI must use https://, or http:// with localhost or 127.0.0.1, and an exact host; see Custom MCP clients.
57: - [Monetary Values](/llms-guides/monetary-values.txt) - Most Ramp API monetary values use integers in the smallest denomination of the relevant currency. The field names and supported currency identifiers depend on the endpoint's schema. Standard currencies such as USD, EUR, and JPY use ISO 4217 codes. Some schemas also support stablecoin identifiers such as USDC, which can be used for eligible stablecoin Bill Pay payments. A currency's presence in a schema does not mean every payment method supports it.
58: - [Pagination](/llms-guides/pagination.txt) - Pagination allows you to retrieve an entire dataset with a series of requests, where each request fetches a portion of the data set. By loading data in smaller chunks, pagination reduces the amount of data transmitted per response and alleviates the load on the servers, ensuring faster loading times and a smoother user experience.
59: - [Procurement](/llms-guides/procurement.txt) - Bring procurement requests, approvals, and purchase orders into your stack — so the system that already drives intake or approvals stays the source of truth.
60: - [Procurement Integrations with the Blank Canvas API](/llms-guides/procurement-intake.txt) - Route Ramp intake requests through your own procurement or contract management system — receive each request via webhook, run your review, and send the approval decision back through Blank Canvas.
61: - [Ramp Data MCP](/llms-guides/ramp-data-mcp.txt) - The Ramp Data MCP server exposes Ramp's datasets — Ramp Rate software benchmarks and AI Index business AI adoption metrics — to MCP-compatible clients.
62: - [Ramp MCP](/llms-guides/ramp-mcp.txt) - Ramp MCP connects AI tools such as Claude, ChatGPT, and Cursor to your Ramp account. Each connection acts as the signed-in user, with that user's Ramp permissions.
63: - [Ramp Rate](/llms-guides/ramp-rate.txt) - Ramp Rate is subject to change. Feedback and questions can be submitted via a Developer API support ticket.
64: - [Rate Limits and Timeouts](/llms-guides/rate-limiting.txt) - A 504 Gateway Timeout means a gateway did not receive an upstream response before its timeout. Avoid relying on long-running requests when working with large datasets or complex queries:
65: - [Reimbursements](/llms-guides/reimbursements.txt) - Pay employees back for out-of-pocket expenses — manual submissions, OCR'd receipts, and mileage — gated by funds, routed through approvals, and synced to your ERP.
66: - [Sandbox](/llms-guides/sandbox.txt) - The Ramp sandbox is a testing environment where developers and partners can safely build, test, and experiment with Ramp's API without affecting live production data.
67: - [Get Sandbox Access](/llms-guides/sandbox-access.txt) - No summary
68: - [Spend Controls](/llms-guides/spend-controls.txt) - Budgets, templates, and approval workflows control Ramp spending. The controls that apply depend on the payment method and product.
69: - [Spend Programs](/llms-guides/spend-programs.txt) - Compose Ramp's spend control primitives — funds, spend programs, transactions, webhooks — to manage a recurring budget end-to-end: stamp out funds from a template, share them across a team, watch the spend in real time, and wind down cleanly when the cycle ends.
70: - [Technology Partnerships Application](/llms-guides/technology-partnerships.txt) - No summary
71: - [User lifecycle](/llms-guides/user-lifecycle.txt) - Onboard, update, deactivate, reactivate, and stage draft users through the Users API. Three scenarios cover the common provisioning paths between Ramp and your HRIS or IdP.
72: - [Users](/llms-guides/users.txt) - The people on a Ramp account — provisioned, updated, deactivated through the Users API. Users are the principal behind every spend object.
73: - [Virtual Cards](/llms-guides/virtual-cards.txt) - Virtual cards are fund-backed cards. Choose Embedded Cards when a person enters card details, or the Vault API for an approved backend flow.
74: - [Webhooks](/llms-guides/webhooks.txt) - Webhooks allow your application to receive real-time notifications about events that occur in your Ramp account. Instead of polling our API, webhooks push notifications to your specified endpoint whenever an event happens.
75: ## API Reference
76: - [OpenAPI spec](/openapi/developer-api.json) - Canonical OpenAPI schema.
77: - [Plain-text API reference](/llms-api.txt) - Generated endpoint and schema reference.
78: ## Full Exports
79: - [Plain-text guides index](/llms-guides.txt) - All guides in one file.
80: - [Combined guides and API reference](/llms-full.txt) - Single file with both guides and endpoint reference.

10122: title: Create a token
10123: path: /developer/v1/token
10124: description: Expects two headers:
10125: - Authorization header formed from base-64 encoded client credentials as `Authorization: Basic <base64-encoded client_id:client_secret>`
10126: - `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded`
10127: Required content body depends on authorization type method, as defined by `grant_type`.
10128: - Authorization Code Grant (`grant_type=authorization_code`): `grant_type`, `code`, and `redirect_uri` are required. Request must happen after requested scopes have been approved and exchanged for authorization code.
10129: - Refresh Token Grant (`grant_type=refresh_token`): `grant_type` and `refresh_token` are required. User must have previously obtained refresh token in authorization code flow.
10130: - Client Credentials Grant (`grant_type=client_credentials`): `grant_type` is required. If `scope` is omitted, the access token has no scopes.
10131: - JWT Bearer Grant (`grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer`): `grant_type` and an ID-JAG `assertion` are required. Issues a user-level access token without a refresh token.
10132: request: {
10133: assertion?: string
10134: code?: string
10135: grant_type: 'authorization_code' | 'client_credentials' | 'refresh_token' | 'urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer'
10136: redirect_uri?: string
10137: refresh_token?: string
10138: scope?: string
10139: }
10140: response: {
10141: access_token?: string
10142: expires_in?: number
10143: id_token?: string
10144: refresh_token?: string
10145: refresh_token_expires_in?: number | null
10146: resource?: string | null
10147: scope?: string
10148: token_type?: string
10149: }
10150: ---
10151: title: Revoke an access or refresh token
10152: path: /developer/v1/token/revoke
10153: description: Expects an authorization header formed from base-64 encoded client credentials as `Authorization: Basic <base64-encoded client_id:client_secret>`.
10154: Content body must be form-encoded. Example:
10155: ```
10156: curl \
10157: -X POST \
10158: -H "Authorization: Basic <base64-encoded client_id:client_secret>" \
10159: -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \
10160: --data-urlencode 'token=$RAMP_API_TOKEN' \
10161: 'https://api.ramp.com/developer/v1/token/revoke'
10162: ```
10163: request: {
10164: token: string

11387: title: Create a procurement request
11388: path: /developer/v1/unified-requests
11389: description: Early access: enabled per business. Requires a business-scoped token.
11390: Purchase-order and approval-only procurement spend programs are
11391: supported; the request is created for `request_owner_id`. Pass
11392: `submit: false` to create a draft without submitting it; otherwise, the
11393: request is submitted into that program's approval flow by default. File-upload
11394: form fields are not supported: a program whose form requires one cannot
11395: be submitted through this endpoint, and the field is reported in
11396: `additional_info.fields_to_answer`.
11397: A vendor answer with `new_vendor_name` may include
11398: `new_vendor_contact: {"email": "contact@example.com"}`. The contact is
11399: saved as the new vendor's default before submission, including for drafts.
11400: No separate contact field is needed on the program's form.
11401: Set `request_blanket_purchase_order: true` to request a blanket PO, and
11402: `is_total_amount_estimated` to mark the total as an estimate. Each is
11403: rejected with `DEVELOPER_7195` when the program doesn't show its
11404: question; `additional_info.validation_errors[].field_id` names the field.
11405: Returns the request detail. Request-level selections appear under
11406: `purchase_order.accounting_tracking_category_selections`
11407: (`tracking_category.uuid` = `accounting_field_id`,
11408: `tracking_category_option.uuid` = `accounting_field_option_id`). Lines
11409: appear under `purchase_order.purchase_order_line_item_log_entries` with
11410: their `id`, `accounting_tracking_category_selections`, and
11411: `custom_field_values` (`column_id` = `custom_field_id`).

18799: title: Edit a procurement request
18800: path: /developer/v1/unified-requests/{unified_request_id}
18801: description: Edits a native draft or submitted request as its owner. This action never
18802: submits a draft; edits to a submitted request go through normal approval
18803: reconciliation.
18804: How each part of the body is applied:
18805: - Top-level scalars (`name`, `currency`, `entity_id`, `start_date`,
18806: `end_date`): omit to keep the saved value. `start_date` and `end_date`
18807: accept `null` to clear.
18808: - `request_blanket_purchase_order` and `is_total_amount_estimated`: omit to
18809: keep the saved answer, `false` clears it. Each is rejected when the
18810: spend program doesn't show its question for this request.
18811: - `field_answers`: omit to keep all answers. When present, the list is the
18812: complete set of API-editable answers: supported fields not listed are
18813: cleared and `[]` clears them all. File-upload answers are never touched.
18814: - `accounting_field_selections` (request level): omit to keep. When present,
18815: the list is the complete set: enabled fields not listed are cleared and
18816: `[]` clears all.
18817: - `line_items`: omit to keep all lines. When present, the list is the
18818: complete set of lines: a line with `id` is retained and updated, a line
18819: without `id` is created, and any existing line whose `id` is not listed is
18820: deleted. `[]` deletes every line (drafts only; a submitted request must
18821: keep at least one line).
18822: - Every line must carry `unit_price` and `unit_quantity`, and `description`
18823: is written on every call: an omitted or `null` description clears it.
18824: Always re-send `id` and `description` for lines you want to keep.
18825: - A line's `accounting_field_selections` and `custom_field_values` follow
18826: the collection rule: omit to keep the retained line's saved coding, send
18827: the complete list to replace it (enabled fields not listed are cleared),
18828: or send `[]` to clear it.
18829: Returns the request detail. Request-level selections appear under
18830: `purchase_order.accounting_tracking_category_selections`
18831: (`tracking_category.uuid` = `accounting_field_id`,
18832: `tracking_category_option.uuid` = `accounting_field_option_id`). Lines
18833: appear under `purchase_order.purchase_order_line_item_log_entries` with
18834: their `id`, `accounting_tracking_category_selections`, and
18835: `custom_field_values` (`column_id` = `custom_field_id`).
18836: X-Idempotency-Key is optional; reusing a key rejects the request rather
18837: than replaying the original response.

evidence.observation: quote: The Plaid API is JSON over HTTP. Requests are POST requests, and responses are JSON, with errors indicated in response bodies as error_code and error_type (use these in preference to HTTP status codes for identifying application-level errors). All responses come as standard JSON, with a small subset returning binary data where appropriate. The Plaid API is served over HTTPS TLS v1.2 to ensure data privacy; HTTP and HTTPS with TLS versions other than 1.2 are not supported. Clients must use an up to date root certificate bundle as the only TLS verification path; certificate pinning should never be used. All requests must include a Content-Type of application/json and the body must be valid JSON.

evidence.observation: quote: We recommend sending prompt=consent. The consent screen is where a user who can reach more than one Brex account chooses which account to connect; for example, an external firm like an accountant or bookkeeper can pick between the client accounts they operate on behalf of. Without forcing a selection, the OAuth authorization request would silently skip that screen and the user's primary account may be selected for them. See which account a token represents.

This is a separate concern from account selection: login decides which user signs in, consent decides which of that user's accounts you connect to. You can send both.

evidence.observation: quote: description: Blank canvas workflow steps require the `blank_canvas:write` scope. In a blank canvas workflow, external approval steps can be approved or rejected by the integration. Any other step is approved or rejected as an admin override, which requires the authorized user to have permission to manage workflow approvals (403 otherwise). For blank canvas workflow steps, repeating the action that already completed a step returns 200 without changes, and any other action on a step that is no longer pending returns 409.

evidence.observation: quote: The same endpoint decides the current external approval step of a transaction or reimbursement approval chain, which requires the `approvals:write` scope. Transaction steps support `approve` and `request_revision`, which requires a `reason`. Reimbursement steps support `approve` and `reject`, which requires a `reason`. A repeated or stale decision on a transaction or reimbursement step returns 409.

evidence_rules:
# Research format and evidence rules

Contract version 1.1, 2026-11-23 (updated in Task 06 from v1.0 based on verified Task 05 pilot findings; sealed v1.0 runs retain their frozen contract snapshots).

### Changelog (v1.0 → v1.1)
- Added `vendor_approval_required` to `credential_eligibility.{testing,production}` to separate platform/vendor API-access review (e.g., Google Ads Explorer/Basic/Standard application) from commercial/agency `partner_approval_required`.
- Clarified edition-matching for `mcp.discovery`: a community MCP targeting a different product edition (e.g., personal web/cookie scraping vs. Enterprise REST API) must not assert `found` for the Enterprise scope without explicit edition alignment.
- Reinforced per-claim attachment: every material detail in a claim (including `purpose` and MCP tool-list observations) must be anchored inside that claim's own attached evidence array and locator line range.

## Files and migration

- `data/apps.json` is the 100-app identity roster, in assignment order. Its provenance identifies the original conversation and user turn. Original app/hint Markdown is retained verbatim, including link targets and parenthetical hints. Categories and normalized names match the audited roster.
- `legacy_candidate_doc_urls` preserves the scaffold's URL leads with their separate provenance. Neither these URLs nor assignment hints establish auth, access, API or MCP findings. Do not inherit the old OAUTH/APIKEY/GATED/MCP lists, generic descriptions, breadth placeholders or buildability labels.
- `schemas/record.json` is a Draft 2020-12 schema for one app in one immutable run. `examples/unresearched-record.json` is a format example, excluded from research and accuracy totals.
- Initialize substantive claims as `not_researched`, with null values and empty evidence. Keep prior artifacts intact as legacy material; a migration must not relabel their guesses as documentary observations. Existing scripts do not yet consume or enforce this contract.
- Paygent Connect (84) is unresolved. Preserve the original `paygent (NMI-powered)` hint. The legacy paygentglobal.com lead has no established identity match. Resolve vendor/product/edition with primary evidence before attaching that domain's facts; do not substitute a similarly named payment company. The example intentionally leaves this unresolved.

## Claim states and evidence

Each scalar claim has a stable `claim_id`, `status`, `value`, `context`, `evidence`, `supporting_claim_refs` and `rationale`. Context names the edition, API version, account type, region and environment where relevant; say which details remain unknown. IDs remain stable across revisions for the same question. Split materially different scopes into distinct method/entry claims rather than merging them.

| Status | Meaning and counting |
| --- | --- |
| `observed` | Explicitly supported by captured source content; non-null value and evidence required. This means documentary observation, not verified truth or a successful API call. |
| `inferred` | Reasoned conclusion; non-null value, evidence, rationale and supporting claim references required. Report separately from documentary observations. |
| `unknown` | Attempted investigation did not resolve the question. Null value; explain the gap. |
| `disputed` | Conflicting content has not been reconciled. Null value; at least two evidence observations and an explanation required. |
| `not_researched` | No investigation yet. Null value; never count as a finding. |
| `not_applicable` | Evidence explains why the question does not apply to the stated scope. Null value; not a negative result or a correct auth/access claim. |
| `not_found_in_checked_sources` | A bounded search found no supported result. Null value and evidence identifying checked content/search scope required. Use for MCP discovery; never translate to 'no MCP exists'. |

`coverage_status` on auth/protocol/resource collections is workflow metadata: `not_researched`, `partial`, or `checked_sources`. `checked_sources` means only the listed sources were examined, never exhaustive coverage of the vendor. Empty arrays do not prove absence. Record unresolved questions in `notes`; a researched collection can still be incomplete.

For each evidence observation record:

- The actual source URL, source kind, exact heading/anchor, page/line range, or repository path plus commit and line range in `locator`.
- A short captured observation or faithful paraphrase supporting this specific claim. A homepage URL, search-result snippet, or a whole-page citation without a locator is a lead, not substantive evidence.
- `captured_on` (ISO date), capture method, and document date/version when known. Null document metadata means unknown, not current. Capture dates must reflect actual reading, not run creation.
- SHA-256 of the captured content and a relative `snapshot_ref` where feasible. Hash normalized/extracted content only if the snapshot is exactly that content and the extraction method is recorded. If no content snapshot/hash is available, use null and a specific `hash_unavailable_reason`; do not fabricate a digest. A hash proves content identity, not correctness. Never store credentials in snapshots.

For actual operational tests, use `source_kind: execution_receipt` and `capture_method: execution_log`. These require a real local receipt/log in `snapshot_ref` and its SHA-256; `source_url` may be null for a local log. Its locator identifies the run/tool call and relevant log lines; observation states the actual result. This is the only source kind that allows a null source URL. This format permits future receipts; it implements no execution functionality and the Task 02 example has no operational findings.

Prefer vendor developer/auth/pricing/access docs and official repositories. Community repositories support their own implementation claims, not vendor endorsement. Assignment text supports identity/category/hints only. Cite approval and pricing sources for eligibility claims; an API reference alone need not establish a free credential path. If official sources conflict, preserve both observations and their time, version and scope; do not silently pick one. `conflicts` links the affected claim IDs and explains the discrepancy; `disputed` claims may also hold both observations directly.

Evidence is attached per claim. Each auth method, API protocol, resource group and MCP entry has its own claim and evidence. A shared page may be cited repeatedly with the appropriate locator. One citation must not silently support other array members or scopes. When one claim necessarily includes several details (e.g. an auth method plus documented scopes), its evidence must support every detail; otherwise split the claim or omit unestablished optional details. For review, any unsupported material detail makes that whole claim unsupported; do not inflate the denominator by splitting punctuation into claims.

## Field rules

**Identity and purpose.** `identity.id`, `app` and `category` come from the roster; resolve product identity in `identity.resolution` using a cited product/edition description. Category is assignment metadata, not a researched auth claim. `purpose` is a short, single-line, cited description. Do not put placeholder prose in an observed value.

**Auth.** `auth.items` contains a separate claim per method and scope. Preserve OAuth2, API key, Basic and tokens separately; don't choose a single winner. `context` and `details` explain API/edition/actor, OAuth grant or signing scheme; `scopes` lists only documented scopes relevant to the described use. An empty scopes list means no scopes captured, not unrestricted permissions. For CLI/local software, only assert `none` or `not_applicable` when supported for that interface; lack of a REST API does not settle CLI buildability.

**Credentials.** `credential_eligibility.testing` and `.production` each contain independent boolean claims:

- `free_access`, `trial_access`, `sandbox_access`: true means a documented credential/use path is available for this environment; false requires evidence of its absence or inapplicability. Unknown stays null.
- `paid_required`, `admin_approval_required`, `vendor_approval_required`, `partner_approval_required`, `contact_sales_required`: true means this condition is required for the stated path/scope. False needs explicit support for proceeding without it; silence is unknown. Distinguish `vendor_approval_required` (vendor/platform API-access review or application, such as Google Ads Explorer/Basic/Standard) from `partner_approval_required` (commercial, agency, or technology partnership program gating) and `admin_approval_required` (customer tenant/organization admin role or approval).
- `self_serve`: a documented path allows the intended developer to obtain the relevant credentials without vendor/partner intervention. A paid path may be self-serve; an existing tenant's admin can still be required. State actor/plan/prerequisites in each claim's context. Never derive this by default or from 'Sign up'.

These conditions can coexist. A free sandbox can require admin approval; production may require a paid account and partner approval. For alternative credential paths, the context of each claim must identify exactly which path it describes. Do not collapse conflicting paths to one app-wide boolean: use unknown/disputed with explanatory evidence until a scoped answer is possible. A paid product does not automatically mean API access is gated, and a free trial does not establish production access.

**API surface.** Protocols, public documentation, resource groups and breadth are independent claims. A known REST protocol must survive even when breadth and resource groups are unknown. Record each documented protocol and resource group separately with supporting sections; a source can establish 'contacts' while leaving 'billing' unresearched. `public_documentation` refers to documentation visibility for this API scope, not credential eligibility or public data access. Public documentation does not mean anonymous API access.

`breadth` is an inference supported by resource-group claim IDs: `narrow` = one focused workflow/group; `moderate` = multiple related groups; `broad` = multiple distinct business domains. Explain the classification and captured examples in context/rationale. This is qualitative scope, not a fabricated endpoint inventory or a guarantee of completeness. Leave unknown if not enough resource documentation was read. REST/GraphQL/SDK/CLI can coexist; include other interfaces when relevant to agent-callable tools.

**MCP.** `mcp.discovery` is `observed` with value `found` only when at least one supported entry matching the record's declared product edition/scope is recorded. A community MCP targeting a separate consumer/personal edition (e.g., undocumented web-cookie scraping) does not establish `found` for an Enterprise API scope unless tested and documented for that edition; preserve such community entries only with explicit edition separation or leave Enterprise MCP discovery `not_found_in_checked_sources`/`unknown`. Otherwise use the appropriate null state. Each `mcp.entries` item is its own claim with `official`/`community`, source URL, scope, and repository/server URL where established (null otherwise). A server URL may be a hosted endpoint, while a local stdio server may have only a repository URL. No guessed URL. Vendor endorsement must be supported to call it official. Entries for outgoing MCP clients do not establish an app's callable server; record tool direction/scope. `operational_check` remains `not_researched` unless actual execution logs support the result. Docs, a server listing, or a GitHub README cannot establish successful connection, tool calls, or production readiness. This task runs no operational checks.

**Buildability.** This is an explicit inference for a stated agent workflow: `build_now`, `conditional`, `outreach_required` or `not_buildable_for_stated_scope`. Cite supported identity/auth/access/API/MCP or CLI claims through `supporting_claim_refs`, include relevant source evidence, explain the conclusion, list blockers and next steps. A public API can still require outreach; no MCP alone is not a blocker to building an API wrapper. Unknown identity/access/API details can leave buildability unknown. `build_now` is feasibility from evidence, not an implemented or tested integration. Blocker statements also require support; do not label an app unbuildable because a fetch failed.

## Fetch telemetry is separate

`fetches` records URL, attempt date, status, HTTP status, resolved URL, error and optional content digest. It never supplies claim truth. DNS/HTTP errors, login walls, robots blocks and timeouts do not establish no API, paid access, partner gating or nonexistent MCP. A 200 response does not establish a cited claim. Fetch outcomes can prompt follow-up but cannot promote research states automatically.

## Review, runs and accuracy

1. Every saved run gets a unique `run_id`, creation date and producer identity/type. Persist the run input roster hash, schema/rules versions, tool/model versions and configuration alongside that run in a run manifest. Never reuse a run ID or overwrite original records, evidence snapshots, logs or adjudications. The example's run ID is illustrative only.
2. Corrections create a new run with `parent_run_id` and `correction_refs` naming original run/claim IDs plus reasons. Keep the original value/evidence unchanged in the parent; revised claims reuse the same question ID where scope is unchanged. Record added/removed/split claims explicitly in the correction log. New evidence does not retroactively become first-pass evidence.
3. `review` is pending until actual claim adjudications exist. Completed means the listed adjudications are completed, not that every field/app was reviewed. Capture reviewer ID, `ai` or `human`, date, original run ID, each claim ID, judgment, rationale and review evidence. A tool/browser action or another AI is still AI review; only an actual identified person can sign human review. Producer and reviewer identities must be distinct for independent review; disclose shared model/context. Do not copy pending entries over completed reviews.

   An `unresolved` judgment may have an empty evidence array when no source content could be captured. Its required reason must name the actual fetch attempt (for example `fetches[0]` and its date/URL) or an existing failure-log path and describe why adjudication could not finish. Runtime review must resolve that reference. Do not fabricate a source observation for a DNS/access failure. `correct`, `incorrect`, `unsupported` and `not_applicable` judgments still require captured evidence; a failure-only review cannot establish any of them. A completed review containing unresolved judgments does not mean those claims have been verified and contributes no accuracy denominator for those judgments.
4. Before full-run verification, freeze a sampling manifest: manifest ID/path, target run, roster SHA-256, selection date, method/algorithm/version, seed, selected IDs, category counts, reviewer assignments and claim rubric. Use a deterministic seeded selection of two apps per category (20 total), without replacement; report all ten categories including Support and Helpdesk. Preserve pilot/targeted reviews separately from this sample. A seed alone does not reproduce an unspecified algorithm. Do not select actual sample IDs in Task 02.
5. Freeze the claim inventory and scoring rubric before review. Unit = each non-null `observed` or `inferred` claim object, identified by `(run_id, app_id, claim_id)`. Count auth methods, protocols, groups and MCP entries separately; nested operational checks are separate claims only if asserted. Score a compound claim correct only if all material details hold for its scope. Report documentary and inference results separately. Category/roster metadata, example fixtures, collection metadata, null states and bare URLs are not scored findings.
6. Each adjudication is `correct`, `incorrect`, `unsupported`, `unresolved`, or `not_applicable`. Unsupported is a failure to substantiate, not proof of factual falsity. Let C/I/U be completed correct/incorrect/unsupported judgments for asserted claims. Evidence-backed accuracy = C / (C + I + U); print those counts, with unresolved/pending/excluded totals alongside. If the denominator is zero, accuracy is null ('unmeasured'), not 0% or 100%. Exclude null-state claims and not-applicable judgments from this accuracy denominator; report any invalid applicability claims as audit issues. Do not drop incorrect or unsupported results after correction.
7. Report review coverage = completed C/I/U judgments / eligible asserted claims in the frozen sample, with unresolved and pending counts. Separately report research coverage across all 100: counts of observed, inferred and each null state for the six required research areas (purpose, auth, credentials, API, MCP, buildability), plus identity resolution. A collection is not covered just because it exists; distinguish partial protocol knowledge from missing breadth. Report area completion criteria and every denominator. Unknowns do not count as correct findings. No one overall 'accuracy' number should conceal missing research or missing review.
8. First-pass and corrected scores refer to immutable runs, the same sample and the frozen claim questions. Link changed/removed/split/new questions; publish paired results on comparable questions and the changed inventory separately. Do not claim improvement by deleting hard claims, changing denominators or relabeling a failure unknown. A corrected/previously reviewed sample is not an unbiased held-out estimate; disclose reuse. Report no accuracy or improvement until actual adjudication exists. Prepare a human checklist if no person has reviewed yet; do not claim human checks were performed.

## Publication contract (later tasks only)

A hosting config, Site registration, expected URL, local Git directory or ZIP is not proof of publication. Save a repository creation/write receipt, actual repository URL, commit SHA, source/README existence and readback evidence. Save the deployment ID/status, actual live URL, deployed commit or artifact SHA-256, date, and an independent fetch/browser result demonstrating the page is accessible to the intended reviewer. Record real errors/blockers when unsuccessful. No publication is attempted in Task 02.

No dependencies were installed. From the workspace root, the available PowerShell validates the example:

```powershell

It cannot establish source truth, identity, evidence relevance, all reference integrity, actual human activity, or immutable run history.
